articles.title: Joint Resource Exploration With China a ‘Possibility’ Before 2028, Philippine President Says
articles.full_text:
Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said that Manila and Beijing have made progress in energy talks, despite the ongoing tensions in the South China Sea.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. takes part in a luncheon with foreign journalists in Manila, Philippines, Aug. 14, 2026.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. says that joint offshore oil and gas exploration with China remains a “distinct possibility” before the end of his term in 2028, despite the recent intensification of their disputes in the South China Sea.
Speaking at a foreign media luncheon in Manila on Friday, Marcos said that Manila and Beijing were making progress in talks on the matter, and that the U.S.-Israel-Iran war had highlighted Manila’s need to shore up its energy security.
“The Philippines needs additional supplies of oil and gas, and we need to explore the possibilities that we have in the Philippines, in the West Philippine Sea, and wherever else we can [that] we can take advantage of,” he said, as per Rappler.
In March, Marcos told Bloomberg Television that the war in the Middle East and the resulting oil supply shock could provide an “impetus for both sides to come to an agreement” after years of friction in disputed waters. The interview aired on the same day that Marcos declared a “national energy emergency” due to the impacts of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which saw a sudden spike in fuel prices.
The two Asian countries then undertook “initial exchanges” on the topic during a meeting between diplomats in late March, which also involved discussions on how to manage disputes in the South China Sea.
“This discussion has gained prominence,” Marcos told reporters. “There were several issues from the beginning that we are slowly working through. And I can see the distinct possibility that there will be such joint explorations.”
Marcos did not mention when a deal could be reached, saying the discussions were still ongoing. “I think the sense that I get is that all parties involved want it to succeed, and that is always a very good sign,” he said.
Marcos’ predecessor Rodrigo Duterte terminated oil and gas exploration talks with China in mid-2022, with then-Foreign Secretary Teodoro Locsin saying that discussions had gone as far as “it is constitutionally possible to go.”
Marcos and Chinese leader Xi Jinping agreed to resume them during Marcos’ state visit to Beijing in early 2023, but have made very little progress due to the intensification of the disputes in the South China Sea. Since taking office, Marcos has openly challenged China’s behavior in Philippine-claimed waters, fortifying security relations with the United States and introducing a “transparency” policy that focused on publicizing the aggressive actions of the China Coast Guard in the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone (EEZ).
As I noted at the time of Marcos’ initial comment, joint exploration of offshore resources (let alone joint development) remains unlikely at the current juncture. Despite Marcos’ call for a “reset” in relations, recent months have seen a rise in tensions between the CCG and Philippine Coast Guard and navy vessels in disputed waters, which culminated on July 20 in a physical altercation between Chinese and Philippine personnel at Second Thomas Shoal in the Spratly Islands.
The Philippines said that one of its personnel sustained a head injury after being struck with a baton by CCG personnel who had deployed in a boat close to the BRP Sierra Madre, the grounded warship that serves as Manila’s outpost on the shoal. China accused the Philippines of attempting to ram the Chinese boat, and of spreading “false propaganda” about the incident. This was followed by two confrontations at Scarborough Shoal, some 650 kilometers to the northeast.
The recent tensions appear to have grown out of the Philippine commemorations of the 10th anniversary of the arbitral ruling handed down by a court of arbitration in The Hague. The ruling found that China’s expansive “nine-dash line,” which asserts Beijing’s sovereignty over nearly all of the South China Sea, had no standing under international law. It also found that Second Thomas Shoal is part of the Philippines’ EEZ and continental shelf. China has dismissed the ruling as “null and void.”
Even if China and the Philippines could reach a deal on joint oil and gas exploration, this would have to surmount considerable constitutional and political hurdles in Manila.
The Philippine Constitution states that “the exploration, development, and utilization of natural resources must remain under the full control and supervision of the State, and may be undertaken only by the State itself or through Filipino citizens or corporations that are at least 60 percent Filipino-owned.”
After Marcos’ initial comment in March, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) stated that any future joint oil and gas exploration with China would “be made solely in accordance with the Philippine Constitution and the country’s laws, jurisprudence and regulations, and in full assertion of its sovereign prerogatives.”

articles.title: How China Is Normalizing Its Presence in the Waters East of Taiwan
articles.full_text:
Accidents, the ‘normalization’ of law enforcement and integration into a sphere of influence
Following the Japan-Philippines Summit Meeting on May 28, 2026, Japan and the Philippines are to hold negotiations to determine the boundaries of their overlapping Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs) and continental shelves in the waters east of Taiwan. The main goals include clarifying the scope of resource development, strengthening defense and maritime security cooperation, and preventing unforeseen clashes. Japan regards this as a model of peaceful resolution under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and consistent with international law; China strongly protests the initiative. Less noted is that the northeastern end of the nine-dash line runs along southeastern Taiwan, and the “2023 edition of China’s standard map,” published by the Ministry of Natural Resources on August 28, 2023, adds a tenth dash line east of Taiwan. This confirms China’s strong interest in those waters. China has also deployed carrier groups there and repeatedly conducted exercises suggesting preparation for an invasion of Taiwan from the east.

Then, in June 2026, China criticized Japan and the Philippines at the same moment the China Coast Guard (CCG) began conducting law enforcement patrols off Taiwan’s eastern coast. articles.title: Indonesia Is the Latest Country to Validate China’s Claim to Taiwan – Unwittingly or Not
articles.full_text:
From Indonesia to Africa and Oceania, China is enlisting foreign countries to support its increasingly strict interpretation of the One China principle.
On the morning of August 12, China’s People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) and an Indonesian Navy warship conducted a joint navigation exercise in the waters east of Taiwan. It was the first time China had exercised with a foreign military in these geopolitically sensitive waters.
The announcement a day earlier had drawn a swift rebuke from Taiwan’s authorities, which called the exercise an act of political manipulation, “aimed at creating a false impression before the international community that the Chinese communists have jurisdiction over waters east of Taiwan.” The United States similarly called on China “to cease its continuous military pressure against Taiwan.”
Chinese state media indeed framed the exercises as evidence of its jurisdiction over the area. The Global Times, a mouthpiece for the Chinese Communist Party, quoted Chinese military affairs expert Zhang Junshe describing the exercise as being of “great significance,” both because it was the first of its kind and because it demonstrated “China’s sovereign rights and jurisdiction over the exclusive economic zone east of Taiwan island.”
The exercise came at a moment when Beijing has increased its operational presence in the waters east of Taiwan in an effort to assert its jurisdiction. After Japan and the Philippines agreed to start delimitation talks over their exclusive economic zones (EEZs), which overlap to the east of Taiwan, China sent Coast Guard and law enforcement vessels to patrol the disputed waters in early June. Although the PLAN has regularly held exercises in these waters, it marked the first time the Coast Guard patrolled the region independently. 
The Coast Guard presence, accompanied by law enforcement and research vessels, were framed as a routine expression of Beijing’s sovereignty over the area. Although initially a special operation, it has now become semi-permanent. And now China is roping in third countries to corroborate its jurisdiction, with state media making this link directly.
In turn, Indonesia’s Navy downplayed the significance of the exercise. Indonesian media reported that the navy confirmed a “limited joint training or passing exercises” with the PLAN on its way back from a joint exercise with Russia in Vladivostok. It added that the vessel in question also conducted similar exercises with Japan’s navy and the U.S. Navy’s Seventh Fleet. 
The press statement seemed to deliberately sidestep the question of jurisdiction, instead referring to Indonesia’s “free and active” foreign policy and the “universal naval tradition conducted when transiting through another country’s maritime area.” A later statement dropped the “country” reference, simply stating “a maritime area” instead. 
It’s difficult to assess whether Indonesia was aware beforehand of the sensitivity of these drills. While Beijing emphasized the significance of the exercises, Jakarta called them routine.
The incident is more evidence of a recent trend where China enlists foreign countries to support its increasingly strict interpretation of the One China principle. The old playbook of China and Taiwan’s diplomatic competition focused on Taiwan’s remaining diplomatic allies and participation in international organizations: Since the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) won the Presidency in 2016, Taiwan has seen the number of diplomatic allies dwindle from 23 to 12. Despite those restrictions, Taipei has proven remarkably flexible and maintains unofficial relations with countries throughout the world. 
However, over the last year Beijing has become more strident in getting other countries to subscribe to its more strict interpretation of its One China principle. As a result, organizations throughout Africa, Oceania, and even in some Western countries have become more hesitant to engage with any official institutions or documents that bear the name Taiwan, or its official name: the Republic of China.
The most notable example of this happened in April, when the Seychelles, Mauritius, and Madagascar revoked overflight clearance to block President Lai Ching-te’s trip to Eswatini, citing their lack of recognition of Taiwan. Although overseas visits have caused tensions between Taiwan and China before, it was the first time third countries were so directly involved in blocking a visit. 
Taiwan’s presidential office blamed Chinese economic coercion. More likely, as the Global South Project argued, these countries spotted an easy opportunity to win points with Beijing, who indeed thanked the countries for abiding by the One-China principle. Eventually, Lai did visit Eswatini after being smuggled in on an Eswatini government airplane. 
Other African countries have also hardened their policies on Taiwan. In June, Kenya confiscated the passports of two Taiwanese academics who traveled there to participate in the Our Oceans Conference, declaring it doesn’t recognize ROC passports. A month earlier, Zambia cancelled RightsCon 2026, a major human rights conference. The organizer cited Chinese pressure over the participation of Taiwanese civil society members. In July, Morocco announced it stopped processing visa confirmation letters for Taiwanese passport holders, causing Taiwanese travelers to cancel their planned visits. Finally, this week, Ugandan officials withheld the passports of several Taiwanese travelers and demanded Chinese passports instead, explicitly citing Uganda’s “One China policy.” In response, Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a travel advisory for Uganda. 
While some of the passport issues were later clarified, the closure of Taipei’s representative office in Papua New Guinea seems to be permanent. In July, Papua New Guinea’s Foreign Minister Justin Tkatchenko abruptly announced the closure of Taiwan’s representative office in Port Moresby to align with the One China policy. Beijing welcomed the decision in a statement published before the official announcement.
The issues of Taiwanese citizens and organizations in Africa and Oceania are examples of China’s grey-zone pressure on Taiwan going global. Under the old playbook, diplomatic switches were clearly attributable to China. Passing exercises, visa issues, and passport quirks are more deniable and reversible; they make it difficult for Taipei to put the blame on a single actor, while Beijing gets international validation that the Republic of China does not exist.
This strategy also has its limits. The Indonesian Navy perhaps did not anticipate becoming a pawn in Beijing’s game, but by refusing to take a clear side it still allowed China to frame the exercise as an endorsement. As a Taiwanese intelligence officer said, “Militarily this does not have a direct impact on Taiwan. It has a geopolitical significance.” While Indonesia gently pushed back, would the next country do the same?

articles.title: Singapore’s Israel Tightrope
articles.full_text:
The city-state’s ties with Israel have been built on a history that very few other Asian countries can boast. But Singapore can still say “no.”
When Singapore gained independence in 1965, it had no army, few resources, and limited room for error. Other countries turned down its requests for military assistance. Israel did not. That history still has relevance as Singapore’s leaders have repeatedly recognized the contribution Israel made at a time when its existence was in jeopardy. 
Over the decades, the relationship expanded from the original defense collaboration to a broader relationship in technology, cybersecurity, research and the life sciences. In 2025, however, Singapore took an unprecedented step: four Israelis faced financial sanctions and travel bans for “egregious acts of extremist violence” against Palestinians in the West Bank, according to the Foreign Ministry.
That decision did not amount to a rupture with Israel, nor did it wipe away the historical appreciation that’s always been a factor in the relationship. Instead, Singapore is communicating that friendship is not synonymous with remaining silent when Israeli actions are at odds with Singapore’s expressed positions on international law and a two-state solution.
Following Singapore’s independence from Malaysia in 1965, the government of Lee Kuan Yew sought assistance from several nations in the development of its military. Israel responded by surveying the island with its advisers and structuring a master plan for building up the Singapore Armed Forces from scratch, namely the “Brown Book.” Singapore’s national service system was also heavily inspired by the Israeli model. This assistance was crucial to the fledgling city-state, as it came at a time when Singapore was at existential risk.
However, for decades, Singapore’s relationship with Israel was a tightly guarded secret. Overt defense cooperation with Israel was a sensitive subject in Southeast Asia, especially the Muslim world, and Singapore knew that such a move could cause tensions with its neighbors. The initial relationship was therefore not explicitly advertised, and political restraint was needed as well as strategic skill. Singaporean officials even referred to the Israeli military advisers who arrived to help build the Singapore Armed Forces by the code name “the Mexicans.”
That tension never went away, although it took a different shape over the decades. In 2025, Singapore’s sanctions on four Israelis once again called attention to the limits of the relationship. The four targeted had been connected to settler violence in the West Bank. Singapore’s stance was unambiguous: Israeli settlements are a violation of international law; their expansion is making a two-state solution more difficult; and acts of settler violence must be contained, with the perpetrators held accountable.
Beyond the sanctions, Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan said that the recognition of a Palestinian state was a question of “when, not if,” while outlining conditions for a Palestinian government, including its acceptance of Israel’s right to exist and rejection of terrorism. Singapore sought to  back both Israel’s survival and statehood for the Palestinians, while condemning settler violence and supporting a negotiated two-state solution. Together, these positions embody Singapore’s approach to diplomacy as a small nation.
International law is not an abstract preference for Singapore. A system where a larger or more powerful state can act without compunction is always dangerous for a small state. In February 2026, Balakrishnan made that argument in Parliament, saying, “On some issues, we will have to say ‘no’ and to do so courteously, respectfully, and constructively, but nevertheless to stand firm and say ‘no.’ This is not about choosing sides, but about upholding principles and making a careful assessment of Singapore’s long-term national interests.” He connected that to Singapore’s stance in other international conflicts and a broader condemnation of “might is right.” The foreign minister finally concluded: “If we ever lose the ability to say ‘no,’ then that is the day that Singapore loses our relevance and indeed, our independence.”
One the examples Balakrishnan cited was Singapore’s stance on the Israel-Gaza conflict. Singapore wants to rely on international law for its own security; it is difficult for it to stand up for these rules in one war and treat them as bargaining chips in another. The sanctions thus align with a foreign policy tradition, wherein Singapore has kept important ties alive without losing the capacity to disagree with its partners.
Principle, however, is only part of the equation. Singapore sits alongside Muslim-majority Malaysia and Indonesia, which do not recognize Israel. In those states, the Israel-Palestine conflict resonates enough to become a key domestic concern. Muslim Singaporeans are especially attached to the Palestinian cause for religious, humanitarian, and communal reasons, but there is also widespread sympathy for Palestinian suffering across all racial and religious groups. 
The government has been determined to ensure that those feelings are not allowed to boil over into public polarization. In July 2026, Singaporean police investigated two members of the British band Massive Attack after they showed a Palestinian flag and shouted “Free Palestine” during their concert. The musicians were given stern warnings and were not allowed to re-enter Singapore, with the authorities citing concerns over racial and religious harmony. 
The episode showed another part of the Singaporean tightrope. Although pro-Palestinian sentiment is deep-rooted in some sections of society, the government will still make efforts to tightly control the expression of foreign political causes in the local public sphere.
Meanwhile, Singapore’s ties with Israel have grown beyond the initial defense dimension. Singapore has been a regional hub for Israeli companies, and bilateral cooperation has expanded in technology, cybersecurity, life sciences, and industrial research and development. That relationship has pragmatic reasons to continue too, which is why neither side is likely to make a dramatic break. This, too, explains Singapore’s measured reaction. Note that the sanctions targeted individuals rather than the Israeli government or state, while Singapore also stopped short of formally recognizing a Palestinian state, a step b10 countries – including Australia, Canada, France, and the United Kingdom – took in the fall of 2025. 
That said, Singapore is redefining the conditions of the relationship with Israel. While historical gratitude is still relevant, it will not prevent public criticism of Israeli policies when Singapore feels they breach international law or jeopardize a two-state solution.

articles.title: Taiwan Wants to Know Why Indonesia Joined China in a Naval Exercise East of Taiwan
articles.full_text:
The exercise highlighted increasing tensions in the waters east of Taiwan, which are also close to Japan and the Philippines.
This undated photo, released by China’s military, shows the Honghe, the frigate that took part in the passex with Indonesia on Aug. 12, 2026.
In a rare moment of diplomatic friction, Taiwan has called on the Indonesian government to clarify joint naval exercises with China that took place in waters east of Taiwan. 
The exercise took place on the morning of August 12, between 6:30 a.m. and 9:30 a.m. As part of the naval exercise, the Indonesian Navy frigate KRI I Gusti Ngurah Rai and the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy’s Honghe, a guided-missile frigate under the Eastern Theater Command, practiced maritime maneuvers. The drill included practicing formation, maritime communications, as well as replenishment-at-sea, and concluded with a divergence ceremony.
For its part, the Indonesian government has denied that the exercise was threatening in any way. 
“The passing exercises are not war-fighting in nature, but rather a universal naval tradition conducted when passing through the waters of another country,” the Indonesian Navy said in a statement. It described passex activities in general – including, presumably, the one on August 12 – as “goodwill engagements that are commonly conducted by navies around the world as an expression of naval brotherhood and the maritime diplomacy associated with warships.” 
Similarly, the Chinese government claimed that the exercises were in the interests of “jointly safeguarding regional peace and stability.”
Certainly, the scale of the exercise is not to be overstated, as it only involved two vessels. At the same time, according to geointelligence firm ingeniSPACE in a report published by Domino Theory, the exercise took place in Taiwan’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ). The Indonesian vessel, which had its Automatic Identification System (AIS) on, first entered Taiwan’s EEZ before aligning with the Honghe, which did not have its AIS on – as is common for Chinese vessels operating in Taiwan’s EEZ. The Indonesian frigate later passed close to but did not enter Taiwan’s contiguous zone. 
Before its joint exercise with the Honghe, the I Gusti Ngurah Rai had participated in a bilateral exercise, the Orruda 2025, with the Russian navy in late July. After docking at Yokosuka Naval Base in Japan from August 1 to August 8, it later set out for the joint exercise with the PLAN. After that, the Indonesian vessel entered the Philippines’ EEZ and was expected to pass through Scarborough Shoal, a disputed reef claimed by both China and the Philippines. 
Some analysts have read the joint exercise as intended to hit out at increased maritime cooperation between the Philippines and Japan. The two countries held joint exercises with the United States at the end of July in the South China Sea. The drills took place not too long after a renewed round of confrontations between the Philippines and China around Scarborough Shoal, with Manila accusing China of firing water cannons at its vessels, while China hit out at the Philippines for what it claimed was an illegal blockade. 
The Philippines and Japan have increasingly set aside differences in the interests of maritime cooperation as of late. The two countries agreed in late May to delimit their overlapping EEZs and continental shelves in waters east of Taiwan. Such a move may have been aimed at strengthening Japan-Philippines cooperation in the event of a Taiwan contingency.
However, this area also partially overlaps with Taiwan’s EEZ, so Taiwan responded by asserting its own sovereign claims. While Taiwanese political leaders have praised the talks, Taiwan may not want to be left out of talks in which it could be a stakeholder. 
China also objected to the Japan-Philippines talks on the grounds of its claim to control Taiwan – and thus Taiwan’s EEZ. Beijing demanded that Japan and the Philippines “immediately cease all illegal acts that undermine China’s sovereign rights and interests” (referring to the maritime talks) and pledged to “to strengthen control and management over relevant waters.”
China’s joint exercise with Indonesia thus highlighted that the waters east of Taiwan are increasingly a focal point of cross-strait tensions. In June, the China Coast Guard stated that it had stepped up patrols in waters east of Taiwan as a response to the talks between Japan and the Philippines, a move that drew concern from Britain, France, Germany and the United States. China claimed these patrols were in the interests of law enforcement. 
Amid Typhoon Dolphin earlier this month, China’s Guangdong Maritime Safety Administration stated that it would enforce traffic controls on vessels heading northbound in the Taiwan Strait. The Taiwanese government responded by criticizing China for seeking to use the typhoon to reinforce its claims over traffic in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan responded by issuing maritime safety notices through coastal radio and maritime safety centers to reaffirm that the Taiwan Strait is international waters. 
As for Indonesia’s apparent alignment with China in its joint exercise, it is unclear if this reflects a change in policy under the presidency of Prabowo Subianto. In many ways, such alignment would be ironic. Prabowo, previously a former general in Suharto’s New Order regime known for a long-standing record of human rights abuses before his later political career, had been accused in the past of fanning up anti-Chinese sentiment in Indonesia. Consequently, some see him as culpable for the 1998 anti-Chinese race riots that left over 1,000 dead. 
Nevertheless, Prabowo visited China as president-elect. He may be aiming to shed his anti-Chinese image in order to attract economic investment and pacify wary Chinese Indonesian voters domestically. Either way, China is a major economic force in Indonesia, operating factories, mines, and funding Belt and Road Initiative infrastructure projects. 
Prabowo has claimed that he aims to maintain ties of friendship with China, Japan, and the United States alike. However, if he were to rebalance to alignment with China, in many ways Prabowo would be charting the path previously taken by the Philippines’ previous president, Rodrigo Duterte. Amid mounting international criticisms of his bloody war on drugs – for which he is now being prosecuted by the International Criminal Court – Duterte increasingly lashed out at the United States and sought to bring the Philippines’ foreign policy into alignment with China. 
Such moves were later reversed when Ferdinand Marcos Jr. succeeded Duterte as president. Marcos pushed the Philippines back toward closer ties with the United States, as well as Japan. Marcos has also signaled greater interest in ties with Taiwan, congratulating President Lai Ching-te on his election victory in 2024 with a tweet. The Philippines has also made it clear that it sees itself as a stakeholder – or at least implicated – in a potential Taiwan contingency because of the over 150,000 Filipinos residing in Taiwan, mostly blue-collar migrant workers. 
In April, former Philippine Army Vice Commander Leodevic B. Guinid made headlines by stating that interoperability between the Taiwanese and the Philippine militaries would be necessary for evacuations to occur in the event of war. Certainly, a Taiwan contingency could potentially be a major political crisis for any Philippine political leadership, not only because of the economic and geopolitical impact from a distance, but because of the fate of the Filipino population in Taiwan.
Yet Indonesians are by far the largest Southeast Asian group in Taiwan and, in fact, the largest foreign nationality in Taiwan. It is believed that around 350,000 Indonesians reside in Taiwan, also mostly as blue-collar migrant workers. At the same time, there has not been much public discussion to date of what would happen to this group in the event of war in the Taiwan Strait. 
In a rare moment of diplomatic friction, Taiwan has called on the Indonesian government to clarify joint naval exercises with China that took place in waters east of Taiwan. 
The exercise took place on the morning of August 12, between 6:30 a.m. and 9:30 a.m. As part of the naval exercise, the Indonesian Navy frigate KRI I Gusti Ngurah Rai and the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy’s Honghe, a guided-missile frigate under the Eastern Theater Command, practiced maritime maneuvers. The drill included practicing formation, maritime communications, as well as replenishment-at-sea, and concluded with a divergence ceremony.
For its part, the Indonesian government has denied that the exercise was threatening in any way. 
“The passing exercises are not war-fighting in nature, but rather a universal naval tradition conducted when passing through the waters of another country,” the Indonesian Navy said in a statement. It described passex activities in general – including, presumably, the one on August 12 – as “goodwill engagements that are commonly conducted by navies around the world as an expression of naval brotherhood and the maritime diplomacy associated with warships.” 
Similarly, the Chinese government claimed that the exercises were in the interests of “jointly safeguarding regional peace and stability.”
Certainly, the scale of the exercise is not to be overstated, as it only involved two vessels. At the same time, according to geointelligence firm ingeniSPACE in a report published by Domino Theory, the exercise took place in Taiwan’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ). The Indonesian vessel, which had its Automatic Identification System (AIS) on, first entered Taiwan’s EEZ before aligning with the Honghe, which did not have its AIS on – as is common for Chinese vessels operating in Taiwan’s EEZ. The Indonesian frigate later passed close to but did not enter Taiwan’s contiguous zone. 
Before its joint exercise with the Honghe, the I Gusti Ngurah Rai had participated in a bilateral exercise, the Orruda 2025, with the Russian navy in late July. After docking at Yokosuka Naval Base in Japan from August 1 to August 8, it later set out for the joint exercise with the PLAN. After that, the Indonesian vessel entered the Philippines’ EEZ and was expected to pass through Scarborough Shoal, a disputed reef claimed by both China and the Philippines. 
Some analysts have read the joint exercise as intended to hit out at increased maritime cooperation between the Philippines and Japan. The two countries held joint exercises with the United States at the end of July in the South China Sea. The drills took place not too long after a renewed round of confrontations between the Philippines and China around Scarborough Shoal, with Manila accusing China of firing water cannons at its vessels, while China hit out at the Philippines for what it claimed was an illegal blockade. 
The Philippines and Japan have increasingly set aside differences in the interests of maritime cooperation as of late. The two countries agreed in late May to delimit their overlapping EEZs and continental shelves in waters east of Taiwan. Such a move may have been aimed at strengthening Japan-Philippines cooperation in the event of a Taiwan contingency.
articles.summary: The exercise highlighted increasing tensions in the waters east of Taiwan, which are also close to Japan and the Philippines.

articles.title: Why India Needs a Comprehensive Polar Strategy
articles.full_text:
The Arctic and Antarctic are reshaping both the global climate and the geopolitical chessboard. Yet India remains absent from the tables where polar futures are decided.
A helicopter carries the Indian flag while passing over India’s Maitri research station in Antarctica, Feb. 2, 2005.
For generations, India’s strategic policies have been anchored by two geographical features: the Himalayas guarding its northern boundaries and the Indian Ocean protecting its maritime boundaries. However, amid renewed scientific and strategic attention as well as great power competitions, other frontiers –  the Arctic Sea and the Antarctic – are quietly redefining the country’s security, economic, and diplomatic landscape.
Against this background, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on External Affairs’ report on “India’s Role and Presence in the Arctic and Antarctic Regions” is more than a routine parliamentary exercise. The committee deemed India’s current approach to the polar region inadequate. It recommended appointing a polar ambassador and creating a dedicated Polar Affairs Desk within the Ministry of External Affairs to strengthen capability and pursue a more proactive diplomatic role in both poles.
While the recommendation deserves support, appointing a dedicated ambassador should be seen only as a beginning for India’s polar presence. What New Delhi requires is a comprehensive polar strategy that integrates scientific research with diplomacy, maritime interests, climate security, economic needs, and long-term strategic planning.
India is not a newcomer to the polar regions. It launched the Indian Antarctic Program in 1981 and established a sustained scientific presence through research stations like Dakshin Gangotri (now decommissioned), Maitri, Bharti, and Maitri II (upcoming). In the Arctic, India’s engagement evolved through the establishment of the Himadri research station in Svalbard (2008), then observer status in the Arctic Council (2012), and finally the adoption of India’s Arctic policy in 2022.
While these initiatives have earned India considerable scientific credibility, they also exposed a strategic paradox. India expanded its scientific footprint in the polar regions, but its diplomatic and institutional architecture remains limited. The Arctic states as well as several Arctic Council observer states have polar ambassadors and dedicated institutional mechanisms to coordinate and cooperate in polar diplomacy, scientific research, and strategic planning, something that India clearly lacks.
The Parliamentary Standing Committee rightly identified this institutional gap. Its recommendation clearly indicates that the polar world can no longer be treated only as a niche scientific domain and requires strategic intervention to protect and promote Indian foreign policy interests.
The strongest argument for a comprehensive polar strategy lies not only in distant geopolitics but also in India’s own national interest. The first and foremost reason to pay attention to the poles is climate security. As per reports from the International Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the Arctic is warming nearly four times faster than the global average, causing alterations in atmospheric circulation, ocean systems, and weather patterns across the Northern hemisphere. 
Recent research from the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology showed that the declining Arctic sea ice is influencing Indian monsoons by altering Rossby waves and the Asian jet stream. The impact of this extends beyond climatology and impacts Indian agriculture, food security, water management, and disaster preparedness. Further, the cryosphere – i.e. the Arctic, the Antarctic and the Himalayan regions – forms an interconnected climate system. Accelerated melting of ice, whether of Himalayan glaciers or at the poles, contributes to sea level rise, threatening around 11,000 kilometers of India’s coastline and island territories.
The second reason India should care about the poles is maritime connectivity. More than 90 percent of India’s merchandise trade by volume is transported by sea. With a changing climate, the Northern Sea Route through the Arctic is becoming more navigable, and that can influence global shipping economics, logistics, and supply chains. India, whose maritime vision is reflected through initiatives like SAGAR and transit corridors like the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), can no longer view developments in the Arctic in isolation.
The third dimension to this lies in geoeconomics. The polar region holds significant reserves of hydrocarbons, fisheries, and critical minerals essential for renewable energy technology and other strategic industries. International resource and environmental safeguards will continue to regulate the utilization of polar resources. A country like India, in pursuit of resilient supply chains, self-reliance, and energy security, can’t afford to remain absent from these discussions, and hence requires a comprehensive polar strategy.
If climate change provides the environmental rationale for polar engagement, and economics adds value to the proposition, geopolitics provides the strategic imperative. 
In recent years, the Arctic has evolved from a scientific frontier to a new arena of strategic competition. Russia transformed the Northern Sea Route into a key economic corridor and is strengthening its military base across the region, whereas NATO has renewed its focus on the High North following recent European security developments. China has been particularly proactive in the Arctic since issuing its Arctic White Paper (2018), which described China as a “near Arctic” country and proposed the Polar Silk Road as an expansion to the Belt and Road Initiative. 
The interests of New Delhi differ fundamentally from its peers, as it seeks neither  territorial influence nor resource competition, but believes in scientific credibility and a rule-based international order. However, one lesson is clear: to ensure influence and resource security, India requires sustained institutions and strategy dedicated to the poles.
Unlike the Arctic, Antarctica is governed through the Antarctic Treaty System of 1959, which reserves the continent for peaceful scientific purposes. India signed this treaty in 1983 and attained consultative party status in the system. However, today Antarctica can no longer be viewed solely through a scientific lens. Questions related to biodiversity, marine areas, resource management, and environmental governance are becoming equally important. Here, India’s decade-long scientific presence places the government in a leading position to advocate balance and a rule-based order in Antarctica and its overall safeguard as a global commons.
Further, India’s engagement with the polar regions should not be viewed solely through the lens of great power competition. Since the Non Alignment Movement, India has positioned itself as a leading voice of the Global South. With that history in mind, India brings a distinct perspective to polar governance, advocating for equity, sustainability, and inclusive multilateralism. 
The consequences of Arctic warming and Antarctic degradation are not limited to polar states; rather it disproportionately impacts developing countries through changing monsoon patterns, climate-induced disasters. Most of these countries lack influence and capacity to counter these issues. India in this situation, is positioned uniquely to bridge this gap through its scientific presence, diplomatic weight, and longstanding advocacy for climate justice, enabling it to push for a framework that reflects the concern of climate vulnerable states. 
This requires India not to treat the polar regions as an arena of scientific experiment alone, but instead push for responsible stewardship with the spirit of Vasudhaiva Kutumbkam. In its polar strategy, India should act as a bridge between the developed and developing world.
By the above analysis, it can be said that a comprehensive polar strategy is the need of the hour for India to fulfill its national interests in a number of areas, be it climate security, energy security, great power competition or Global South politics. For India, however, a mere scientific presence is not enough; rather it requires strategic influence in the region.
The Parliamentary Stand Committee recommended that India appoint a Polar Ambassador, establish a Polar Affairs Desk at the Ministry of External Affairs, and acquire a polar research vessel, among others. These points deserve serious consideration. Following the recommendations will provide continuity and coordination in diplomacy, deepen India’s engagement with Arctic and Antarctic partners, and ensure consistent representation in decision-making forums.
However, diplomacy without a comprehensive strategy risks becoming symbolic. India already laid a foundation through its Arctic Policy of 2022. What it needs now is to translate these policies into an actionable strategy integrating both the Arctic and Antarctic in a single strategic framework.
First, India should establish a National Polar Coordination Mechanism by bringing related ministries like External Affairs, Defense, Shipping, Earth Science, and Environment for coordinated policymaking. Second, India should strengthen scientific leadership through the acquisition of modern research vessels, timely completion of Maitri II, and enhanced climate modeling and satellite observation. Third, India should institutionalize polar diplomacy by increasing cooperation with the Nordic states, Japan, South Korea, and other like-minded countries. Fourth, India should invest in strategic capacity by promoting research, scholarship in polar geopolitics, environmental governance, and maritime law across universities and policy institutions.
Fifth and finally, India should redefine its strategic geography, where the Arctic and Antarctic shall be part of India’s extended neighborhood, transcending conventional geographical boundaries. Development in these regions directly impact India’s security, economy, and environment; it’s time for India’s strategy to reflect that reality.
Ultimately, India’s polar engagement should not be measured by the number of research stations it operates or diplomatic positions it creates. Rather it should be evaluated based upon India’s ability to influence or shape polar governance. The Parliamentary Standing Committee’s recommendations provide an opportunity to move from scientific presence to strategic positioning by leveraging its scientific credibility, diplomatic capacity, and leadership. 
The Arctic and Antarctic may lie far beyond India’s territorial boundaries but in the near future these regions will shape India’s climate, economy, and security. Hence, the time has come for India to look beyond the Himalayas and take necessary steps for a comprehensive polar strategy.

However, amid renewed scientific and strategic attention as well as great power competitions, other frontiers –  the Arctic Sea and the Antarctic – are quietly redefining the country’s security, economic, and diplomatic landscape.

While the recommendation deserves support, appointing a dedicated ambassador should be seen only as a beginning for India’s polar presence. What New Delhi requires is a comprehensive polar strategy that integrates scientific research with diplomacy, maritime interests, climate security, economic needs, and long-term strategic planning.

articles.title: In Interview, Japarov Says He’d Planned for Tashiev to Be Kyrgyz President Next
articles.full_text:
Japarov claimed he changed his mind once he realized Tashiev is “not ready.”
Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov claimed in an August 13 interview with journalist Ali Toktakunov that he’d planned for his former ally and security chief Kamshubek Tashiev to follow him in the presidency, but changed course once he realized “he’s not ready.”
The revelation comes in tandem with Kyrgyzstan’s prosecutor general appealing the July verdict and sentences in the “Letter of 75” case, seeking harsher punishments. 
Japarov also clarified in the interview that he will, indeed, seek a second term in January in order to “complete” his reforms. 
Tashiev served as the head of the State Committee for National Security (SCNS) until his surprising dismissal in February. At the time, Japarov explained the dismissal of his friend and close ally as necessary to “strengthen the unity of the state and prevent divisions in society, including between government agencies.”
A month before his dismissal, Tashiev had responded to mounting rumors that he would seek the presidency. “Many have tried and continue to try to sow discord between us, claiming that I aspire to the presidency. But this is not true,” he said at the time. “I do not intend to overthrow Sadyr Nurgoyevich h [Japarov]… In this life, only death can separate us.”
Tahsiev has consistently denied any ambition to become president, even as he built up a resume of successes and consolidated power around himself. But Japarov just said he intended to retire after his first term and pass the presidency on to Tashiev. 
So what happened? According to Japarov, he’d told Tashiev, “Be prepared, cleanse your circle, educate your people.” Tashiev apparently did not do so.
“Then I see: he’s not ready,” Japarov continued. “His staff isn’t behaving as expected, and people in his entourage have skyrocketed in power.” When the “Letter of 75” appeared, Japarov said, “When parliament began to be divided between the general’s supporters, I summoned him and said: ‘This is unacceptable. You can’t divide the people. I will severely punish those who divide the people into north and south, because the people have only just begun to unite. So don’t be offended, I’m removing you from your post.’”
There’s an ironic precedent for all of this: Japarov’s predecessor, Sooronbai Jeenbekov was the hand-picked successor of his predecessor, Almazbek Atambayev. Their falling out, which intensified in 2019 with Atambayev’s arrest, threw Kyrgyzstan into the political chaos that saw Japarov busted from prison and swept into the presidency in 2020. Tashiev, long an ally of Japarov’s, rose with him into power. And then it all fell apart.
Tashiev, alongside former Speaker of the Zhogorku Kenesh Nurlanbek Turgunbek uulu, former Member of Parliament Kurmankul Zulushev, and five others, were found guilty last month of a coup attempt under Article 326 (“Violent seizure or retention of power, as well as an attempt to violently change the constitutional order”) and acquitted of abuse of office charges.
The prosecutors had sought nine-year sentences. Tashiev and the rest were sentenced to four years in prison, but the judge replaced their prison terms with three years of supervised probation. The five defendants who had been in custody were released. Tashiev served not a single day in detention.
On August 13, the same day Japarov’s interview was posted to YouTube, the Prosecutor General’s Office appealed the verdict. According to Tashiev’s lawyer, as reported by 24.kg, the prosecutor is requesting that the acquittal portion of the verdict be overturned and that due punishment be imposed. Additionally, the prosecutor argues that the sentences under the Article 326 charge are too lenient and should be increased.
The defendants are seeking a full acquittal. 
Kyrgyzstan is set to hold presidential elections in January 2027. As early as January 2024, Japarov’s allies were floating the possibility of him seeking a second term. Then-Deputy Prime Minister Edil Baisalov – now Kyrgyzstan’s ambassador to the United States – told RFE/RL that the Kyrgyz constitution allowed for a second term and that Japarov would “not just abandon things halfway.”
One aspect of the political upheaval earlier this year in Kyrgyzstan was a rumbling in certain quarters in favor of an early presidential election. That was a core piece of the “Letter of 75.” 
Kyrgyzstan’s Constitutional Court weighed in quickly, arguing that the presidential election could not be held early – and also that Japarov’s current term counts as the first of two permitted under the current constitution, approved via referendum in April 2021.
In late July, Japarov signed a bill into law that altered the election schedule, though it merely served to move the vote from January 24 to January 27 – shifting from the fourth Sunday of the month to the fourth Wednesday. 
In his recent interview, Japarov said the door was open for anyone to run against him: “Anyone who wants to run for office can do so. As they say, go ahead. We won’t restrict anyone. The elections will be transparent, and there will be no obstacles for competitors.”
There may be one obstacle for Tashiev and his fellow defendants: It’s hard to run for office from prison. In fact, under 2025 legislation that Japarov signed off on, individuals with criminal records are barred from running for president entirely.

articles.title: China Forced Nepal to Cancel an International Conference on Tibetan Studies
articles.full_text:
The incident reveals Beijing’s growing efforts to assert authority over Tibetan Buddhism – including in other countries.
The 17th Seminar of the International Association for Tibetan Studies (IATS) Conference, scheduled to be held at Kathmandu University, Nepal, from August 23-29, was cancelled on August 5 and later shifted online. The cancellation was done by the organizers, at the formal request of the Nepali government. 
The IATS conference is one of the premier academic forums for Tibetan culture, history, language and religion. The conference was set to bring together scholars from 40 countries, including India, China, and the United States – many of whom had already arranged and paid for costs to attend the conference in Kathmandu. The conference had been in planning for four years, as Nepal was selected to host the seminar in 2022. The abrupt cancellation of the conference on grounds of “security concerns” highlights both Beijing’s ironclad grip and bid to assert authority over Tibetan Buddhism. 
The cancellation came after Chinese officials expressed concerns over pro-Tibet activists using the platform for demonstrations. Notably, Nepal’s security agencies had ruled out the possibility of a security threat to the event. 
The pressure came not only from Chinese diplomats but, most remarkably, a religious figure. The Venerable Master Yinshun, former vice president of the Buddhist Association of China and a member of the National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) and abbot of the Chinese Temple of Nepal, visited Nepal on July 29. Following his visit, combined with diplomatic efforts by Chinese Ambassador to Nepal Zhang Maoming, around a dozen scholars from the Tibetan Policy Institute in India withdrew their participation from the conference. 
The cancellation of the conference is consistent with Beijing’s recent efforts to exert control over Nepal’s association with Tibetan Buddhism. This is seen in several pre-emptive and proactive measures taken by Beijing to curb Tibetan Buddhism’s influence in Nepal. Earlier this year, Zhang, China’s ambassador, warned the home minister of Nepal, Sudan Gurung, against any government-level participation by Nepal in the oath-taking ceremony of Penpa Tsering held on May 27 in Dharamshala, India. Tsering is the highest executive authority of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA). Notably, the oath-taking ceremony was also attended by the 14th Dalai Lama.
The CTA functions as the government-in-exile for the Tibetan people globally. Around 91,000 Tibetans registered their vote for the 2026 elections that elected Tsering across India, Nepal, Bhutan, Europe, the United States, and other parts of Asia and Africa. In a bid to delegitimize the elections and the support for the CTA, a Global Times editorial characterized the elections as illegal and the CTA as an illicit “separatist organization.” 
These efforts are not unique to Nepal. China has accelerated its efforts seeking to control narratives and perceptions related to Tibet around the world. Beijing’s bid for control over Tibetan Buddhism in particular comes at a crucial time: the Dalai Lama is now 91 years old, and he has announced that his trust, the Gaden Phodrang, would have the sole authority in recognizing his future reincarnation. Beijing responded swiftly, maintaining that the selection of the Dalai Lama’s successor would be determined by Chinese law. 
The succession of the 14th Dalai Lama poses a strategic challenge to China. The Himalayan landscape spanning across India and China has been the site of border disputes between India and China, most recently the Galwan clashes of 2020. Many locals of the Himalayan region in the states of Sikkim, Ladakh, and Arunachal Pradesh in India are adherents of the Tibetan strand of Buddhism. Notably the Dalai Lama celebrated his 91st birthday in Ladakh – a demonstration of the expanse of influence of the Tibetan strand of Buddhism over the Indian Himalayan landscape. 
The long-established cultural traditions of the locals of the Himalayan region, along with their reverence and faith in the Dalai Lama, delegitimize Chinese claims of normative authority in dictating Tibetan Buddhist practices. China has consistently maintained that the next Dalai Lama will be born in Chinese territory as opposed to the 14th Dalai Lama’s declaration that the next Dalai Lama may be born in India. 
In recent times, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP)  has shown increased attention toward the management of monasteries in its bid to establish control over the Tibetan strand of Buddhism. The CCP has taken on a more intrusive role, as seen during Li Ganjie’s tour of Gansu and Sichuan earlier this year. Li heads the United Front Work Department (UFWD). During the tour, he emphasized legal, standardized management of Tibetan Buddhist institutions and the need for socialist principles to guide Tibetan Buddhism. 
One of the primary tasks of the UFWD in China is to generate favorable receptions for Chinese policies not only domestically but also overseas. In this context, Li’s interest in the management of monasteries is geared toward enhancing the CCP’s control over perceptions of Tibetan Buddhism both at home and abroad. 
In many ways, its attempts to control Tibetan Buddhism expose the CCP’s discomfort with religion in general. An increasing number of the urban middle class in China are turning to religious and spiritual practices. Following the COVID-19 pandemic, a growing number of individuals in China have been attracted to the sense of community that religion provides. Chinese Buddhist institutions are perceived by many as corrupt and criticized for excessive commercialization, whereas Tibetan Buddhism is viewed as more esoteric. This sentiment has grown over the years with the rise in cases of embezzlement and corruption in Chinese Buddhist monasteries and temples. A rising number of the younger population in China are attracted to the day to day practices in Tibetan Buddhism as a key to a more balanced lifestyle.  
Tibetan Buddhism will continue to pose a challenge to China as it aspires to ascendancy in the global order. Despite China’s hawkish diplomatic efforts, normative and moral authority continue to elude Beijing.

This is seen in several pre-emptive and proactive measures taken by Beijing to curb Tibetan Buddhism’s influence in Nepal. Earlier this year, Zhang, China’s ambassador, warned the home minister of Nepal, Sudan Gurung, against any government-level participation by Nepal in the oath-taking ceremony of Penpa Tsering held on May 27 in Dharamshala, India. Tsering is the highest executive authority of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA). Notably, the oath-taking ceremony was also attended by the 14th Dalai Lama.
The CTA functions as the government-in-exile for the Tibetan people globally. Around 91,000 Tibetans registered their vote for the 2026 elections that elected Tsering across India, Nepal, Bhutan, Europe, the United States, and other parts of Asia and Africa. In a bid to delegitimize the elections and the support for the CTA, a Global Times editorial characterized the elections as illegal and the CTA as an illicit “separatist organization.” 
These efforts are not unique to Nepal. China has accelerated its efforts seeking to control narratives and perceptions related to Tibet around the world. Beijing’s bid for control over Tibetan Buddhism in particular comes at a crucial time: the Dalai Lama is now 91 years old, and he has announced that his trust, the Gaden Phodrang, would have the sole authority in recognizing his future reincarnation. Beijing responded swiftly, maintaining that the selection of the Dalai Lama’s successor would be determined by Chinese law. 
The succession of the 14th Dalai Lama poses a strategic challenge to China. The Himalayan landscape spanning across India and China has been the site of border disputes between India and China, most recently the Galwan clashes of 2020. Many locals of the Himalayan region in the states of Sikkim, Ladakh, and Arunachal Pradesh in India are adherents of the Tibetan strand of Buddhism. Notably the Dalai Lama celebrated his 91st birthday in Ladakh – a demonstration of the expanse of influence of the Tibetan strand of Buddhism over the Indian Himalayan landscape. 
The long-established cultural traditions of the locals of the Himalayan region, along with their reverence and faith in the Dalai Lama, delegitimize Chinese claims of normative authority in dictating Tibetan Buddhist practices. China has consistently maintained that the next Dalai Lama will be born in Chinese territory as opposed to the 14th Dalai Lama’s declaration that the next Dalai Lama may be born in India. 
In recent times, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP)  has shown increased attention toward the management of monasteries in its bid to establish control over the Tibetan strand of Buddhism. The CCP has taken on a more intrusive role, as seen during Li Ganjie’s tour of Gansu and Sichuan earlier this year. Li heads the United Front Work Department (UFWD). During the tour, he emphasized legal, standardized management of Tibetan Buddhist institutions and the need for socialist principles to guide Tibetan Buddhism. 
One of the primary tasks of the UFWD in China is to generate favorable receptions for Chinese policies not only domestically but also overseas. In this context, Li’s interest in the management of monasteries is geared toward enhancing the CCP’s control over perceptions of Tibetan Buddhism both at home and abroad. 
In many ways, its attempts to control Tibetan Buddhism expose the CCP’s discomfort with religion in general. An increasing number of the urban middle class in China are turning to religious and spiritual practices. Following the COVID-19 pandemic, a growing number of individuals in China have been attracted to the sense of community that religion provides. Chinese Buddhist institutions are perceived by many as corrupt and criticized for excessive commercialization, whereas Tibetan Buddhism is viewed as more esoteric. This sentiment has grown over the years with the rise in cases of embezzlement and corruption in Chinese Buddhist monasteries and temples. A rising number of the younger population in China are attracted to the day to day practices in Tibetan Buddhism as a key to a more balanced lifestyle.  
Tibetan Buddhism will continue to pose a challenge to China as it aspires to ascendancy in the global order. Despite China’s hawkish diplomatic efforts, normative and moral authority continue to elude Beijing.
The 17th Seminar of the International Association for Tibetan Studies (IATS) Conference, scheduled to be held at Kathmandu University, Nepal, from August 23-29, was cancelled on August 5 and later shifted online. The cancellation was done by the organizers, at the formal request of the Nepali government. 
The IATS conference is one of the premier academic forums for Tibetan culture, history, language and religion. The conference was set to bring together scholars from 40 countries, including India, China, and the United States – many of whom had already arranged and paid for costs to attend the conference in Kathmandu. The conference had been in planning for four years, as Nepal was selected to host the seminar in 2022. The abrupt cancellation of the conference on grounds of “security concerns” highlights both Beijing’s ironclad grip and bid to assert authority over Tibetan Buddhism. 
Rituja Ghosh is an independent researcher based in New Delhi focusing on South Asian politics, China's rise in the global stage, and nontraditional security issues. Her work has been published previously in The Diplomat and the South Asian Monitor.
articles.summary: The incident reveals Beijing’s growing efforts to assert authority over Tibetan Buddhism – including in other countries.

articles.title: In Afghanistan, Growing Resistance Meets Fears of Pakistani Influence
articles.full_text:
Five years after the Taliban’s return, the Afghan resistance is growing but so is the fear of Pakistan’s shadow.
August 15 marks five years since the Taliban returned to power, and throughout that time, the group has presented Afghanistan as a country completely under its control. The small armed opposition in Panjshir, Badakhshan, and Baghlan’s Andarab district has not managed to contest the Taliban’s dominance successfully. 
But the emergence  of new anti-Taliban movements across the country has begun to challenge that image.
Last month, a new resistance group called Sipahiyan-i-Mihan, or “Soldiers of the Homeland,” briefly captured the center of Yaftal-e Payeen district in Badakhshan. Local sources said its fighters entered the district headquarters, disarmed Taliban personnel, and raised their flag. The group withdrew several hours later and said the withdrawal was voluntary, although the Taliban said the fighters fled when reinforcements arrived. 
What neither side could deny was that, for the first time since August 2021, a district center had fallen out of Taliban control. The Taliban later sent reinforcements and prepared a larger operation, but so far, no decisive operation against Sipahiyan-i-Mihan has been publicly reported. 
Other new groups have announced operations as well. This week, the Republic Front of Afghanistan said it had targeted a vehicle carrying the Taliban intelligence chief for Kabul’s 18th district and claimed that he and his companions were killed. Local sources confirmed an explosion, but the casualties remain unverified. The U.S.-based Afghanistan United Front, led by former Afghan army commander General Sami Sadat, also announced “Operation Muharib” and claimed attacks in Kandahar, Helmand, and Badghis. 
Meanwhile, the established National Resistance Front, led by Ahmad Massoud, son of the legendary anti-Taliban commander Ahmad Shah Massoud, and the Afghanistan Freedom Front, led by former army chief General Yasin Zia, have continued and expanded their struggle. For weeks, the Freedom Front and the Taliban have clashed in Badakhshan’s Zebak district. Both claim gains and heavy casualties, although independent verification remains impossible. Residents confirmed days of fighting, Taliban reinforcements, house to house searches, and a frontline visit by the Taliban’s chief of army staff, Fasihuddin Fitrat.
When I spoke by telephone this week with residents of Zebak and Yaftal, their concern was not which side was winning the war, but what militarization had done to their lives.
“Taliban fighters are everywhere, in schools and mosques. They have taken over everything and turned it into their base,” one resident told me.
“We are told to provide food for the Taliban fighters based in our village mosque,” another resident of Zebak said. “But how can we feed them when we can barely feed our own families?”
He was referring to the other war people in Afghanistan are fighting: the war to survive. A May 2026 U.N. Development Program assessment found that three in four Afghans could not meet their basic needs, while more than 80 percent of households were in debt. 
With a quick look at Afghan social media, one can easily see that many anti-Taliban Afghans, both inside the country and in the diaspora, have welcomed the operations by these resistance groups. But their hope is mixed with suspicion. A growing question among some is whether Pakistan, after falling into open conflict with its former Taliban partners, is trying to use the Afghan resistance movements as new instruments of influence.
Mostly, this fear comes from the memory of decades of Pakistan treating Afghanistan less as a sovereign neighbor than as strategic territory to be managed. Pakistan supported the Taliban against the former republic government, and prior to that against the Mujahideen government in the 1990s, always driven by Pakistan’s security calculations, its rivalry with India, and its desire for influence in Kabul. The Taliban were the most successful product of that policy.
Now Pakistan and the Taliban are fighting over the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), cross-border attacks, and the Taliban’s growing engagement with India. 
There are credible signs of political outreach by Pakistan to the Afghan resistance groups, although no public proof that Pakistan is directing or arming any of them. In 2025, Islamabad hosted an Afghan dialogue attended by political figures and women activists while the Taliban were absent. Organizers called it inclusive and not anti-Taliban, but because it took place in Islamabad, it revived suspicions about Pakistan’s intentions. 
Last year, New Lines Magazine reported, citing unnamed sources, that Islamabad had opened channels with opposition representatives and that rumors suggested certain resistance fronts had opened an office in Pakistan. Abdullah Azad Khinjani, head of political affairs for the National Resistance Front, told the magazine that the front remained cautious about Pakistan because the Pakistani establishment historically sought to “manage and contain” Afghanistan’s opposition. 
This is why Afghans  are watching where their political leaders travel, who gives them money, and what commitments they make both in public and in private. Pakistan may want pressure on the Taliban today, but if a post-Taliban government tomorrow refuses to be subservient to Islamabad, what prevents Pakistan from searching for yet another faction to weaken it? That is the cycle the people of Afghanistan fear when it comes to Pakistan. They do not see Pakistan as a well-intentioned neighbor aiming to help resistance groups in Afghanistan build an independent state; they see it as a country that has long helped certain Afghan groups gain power, then turned against Afghanistan when those groups began acting independently. 
Among the armed fronts, the NRF has offered the clearest public framework for relations with Pakistan. Massoud said in an interview that Afghanistan and Pakistan should build an honest strategic relationship based on mutual respect, but he also made clear that he would not accept foreign pressure dictating Afghanistan’s decisions. After Pakistan’s 2026 attacks, he blamed the Taliban’s protection of militant groups for creating regional insecurity, yet rejected foreign bombing and argued that Afghanistan’s freedom must come through a legitimate, Afghan-led national effort. The newer movements discussed here have not publicly set out comparably clear conditions for any engagement with Pakistan.
When I asked a former diplomat, media personality, and supporter of the resistance this week, who wished to remain anonymous, how worried she was that Pakistan might exploit the situation, she said: “Any group that sides with Pakistan, I will not support that resistance group.” 
“Pakistan is bombing our country, claiming it is killing the Taliban, but the people we see killed are civilians. To side with Pakistan means siding with those killing the people of Afghanistan,” she added.
Her anger is grounded in the civilian suffering caused by Pakistani bombings of Afghanistan. The United Nations said at least 28 civilians were killed in Pakistani operations in late June, and Amnesty International later called for an investigation into a March strike on a Kabul drug-treatment facility after UNAMA verified at least 269 civilian deaths. Pakistan maintains that it targeted militants and military facilities.
The resistance supporter, however, did not accept the idea that Pakistan and the Taliban had become natural enemies. 
“They disagree today, but the Taliban are a product of Pakistan,” she said. “Pakistan invested nearly three decades in bringing them to where they are. Even if they are enemies now, that does not mean non-Taliban groups should become Pakistan’s allies. If the resistance takes power and later refuses to become Pakistan’s puppet, Pakistan will bring another group to remove it. This cycle has continued until today.”
“No Afghan faction should allow itself to become a vehicle for another state’s strategic ambitions once again,” she concluded.
On this fifth anniversary, Afghans are not merely looking for someone capable of fighting the Taliban. They are looking for an alternative worthy of replacing them. After five years of repression, with women and girls living under a system increasingly described as gender apartheid and millions struggling to survive, the desire for change is understandable and urgent. But the lesson of Afghanistan’s history is equally important to Afghans because they know that liberation delivered through another country’s machinations can easily become a new form of captivity.
This time, the alternative Afghans are searching for must be built inside Afghanistan, answerable to its people, inclusive of its women and communities, and independent enough to cooperate with neighbors without becoming their instrument of influence. Resistance may begin with removing oppression, but it will deserve the name liberation only if it also breaks the cycle of proxy rule.
August 15 marks five years since the Taliban returned to power, and throughout that time, the group has presented Afghanistan as a country completely under its control. The small armed opposition in Panjshir, Badakhshan, and Baghlan’s Andarab district has not managed to contest the Taliban’s dominance successfully. 
But the emergence  of new anti-Taliban movements across the country has begun to challenge that image.
Last month, a new resistance group called Sipahiyan-i-Mihan, or “Soldiers of the Homeland,” briefly captured the center of Yaftal-e Payeen district in Badakhshan. Local sources said its fighters entered the district headquarters, disarmed Taliban personnel, and raised their flag. The group withdrew several hours later and said the withdrawal was voluntary, although the Taliban said the fighters fled when reinforcements arrived. 
What neither side could deny was that, for the first time since August 2021, a district center had fallen out of Taliban control. The Taliban later sent reinforcements and prepared a larger operation, but so far, no decisive operation against Sipahiyan-i-Mihan has been publicly reported.
