articles.title: 5 Years After the Fall: Why the World Still Misreads the Taliban
articles.full_text:
The international community assumed that governing would change the Taliban. The Taliban, however, viewed government as a means of transforming society according to their ideology.
Armed fighters of the Taliban in Kabul, Aug. 17 2021.
Five years have passed since the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan. During this period, the international community tried a wide range of policies to influence the Taliban’s behavior, from humanitarian assistance and political and economic pressure to diplomatic engagement and negotiations that began through indirect channels and, today, in some cases, have developed into direct talks. 
At the same time, human rights defenders, political opponents of the Taliban, and many ordinary Afghans did not abandon their resistance. From street protests and underground schools to human rights campaigns and various forms of civil disobedience, they sought to prevent the normalization of Taliban rule both within Afghanistan and internationally.
Yet neither the international community’s main expectations nor the hopes of many Afghans were realized. An inclusive government did not emerge, political and social restrictions continued, and rather than becoming more flexible, the Taliban further consolidated their system of rule based on their own ideological interpretation of religion. Women were excluded from education, universities, employment, and much of public life, while civic space and fundamental rights came under even tighter restrictions.
The most common response to this reality has been to conclude: “The Taliban never changed.” But that answer leaves a more important question unresolved. Why were so many international policies based, from the outset, on the assumption that the Taliban would change? Why did a world that had invested two decades in state-building, modern governance, and rule-based institutions in Afghanistan continue to believe that engagement, economic pressure, or the promise of international legitimacy could change the group’s behavior?
Perhaps the central problem was never simply that the Taliban failed to change. Rather, it was that the international community analyzed them through a framework that was ill-suited to understanding the nature of such a movement. The shortcomings of international policy in Afghanistan were not due only to the failure to change the Taliban. Instead, they were rooted in the analytical framework through which the international community understood the movement.
Accordingly, this article does not ask why the Taliban govern as they do. Instead, it asks why, despite the experience of the Taliban’s first regime, two decades of war, and state-building, and five years of direct observation of their rule after returning to power, the international community continued to analyze the movement through a framework that did not fit its actual nature. The answer to this question is important not only for understanding Afghanistan’s recent past, but also for rethinking how ideological movements are analyzed and how future peace processes are designed in other international crises.
How the International Community Understands the Taliban
Much of the international community’s policy toward the Taliban was built on a set of assumptions that ultimately proved inconsistent with the reality of the group’s rule. These policies were shaped by the belief that, after two decades of war, the Taliban’s primary objective was to secure political power, end their international isolation, and become a political actor operating within the established rules of international politics and international relations. It was therefore expected that participation in negotiations, the responsibilities of governing, economic pressure, and the need for international legitimacy would gradually moderate the group’s behavior and priorities.
In practice, this analytical framework rested on three core assumptions. First, that the Taliban understood concepts such as the state, legitimacy, peace, the rule of law, and human rights in the same way these concepts are generally understood in international political and legal discourse. Second, that the transition of an armed movement from the battlefield to a peace process and eventually into government would gradually transform it into an actor compatible with the principles of modern governance. Third, that the responsibilities of governing and the need to engage with the outside world would outweigh the group’s ideological priorities.
These assumptions did not emerge solely from analyses of the Taliban themselves. They also reflected the broader political context of the time. After two decades of war, the international community had grown weary of prolonged conflict, heavy military costs, the failure of the state-building project, and widespread corruption within the former Afghan Republic. In such an environment, reaching a peace agreement became an urgent priority – one that, at times, took precedence over a careful understanding of the Taliban’s nature and the conditions necessary for a durable peace.
The shortcomings of international policy, therefore, cannot be explained simply by tactical mistakes or political optimism. They were rooted in an analytical framework that viewed the Taliban primarily as a political actor rather than as an ideological movement, assuming that holding power would gradually bring the group into line with the demands of modern governance.
From the very beginning of their emergence, the Taliban were less a political actor than an ideological movement with a religious mission. In such movements, governing is not the ultimate goal; rather, it is a means of establishing an order rooted in the movement’s ideological beliefs. Accordingly, the legitimacy of a government is measured not by the consent of citizens or international recognition, but by its fidelity to that mission.
Within this framework, many Taliban policies that appeared costly – or even irrational – to foreign policymakers were entirely consistent with the movement’s internal logic. The Taliban did not merely change the structure of government; they also redefined the concept of citizenship according to loyalty to their own ideological interpretation. The consequences of this approach extended far beyond the exclusion of women from education, employment, and much of public life. Religious and ethnic minorities, intellectuals, civil society activists, independent media, political critics, and many other social groups also faced restrictions and marginalization in public life. 
At the same time, the Taliban strengthened religious institutions, expanded the authority of the Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice, and placed much of the administrative and security structure in the hands of loyal followers. In all these actions, the Taliban demonstrated that they were willing to bear considerable economic, political, and diplomatic costs in areas they regarded as part of their ideological mission.
This does not mean that the Taliban are indifferent to the economy, foreign relations, or the survival of their government. On the contrary, they have shown a pragmatic approach in certain areas, from regional trade to engagement with neighboring countries. However, they draw a clear distinction between what they consider politically negotiable and what they regard as part of their ideological mission. In their view, issues such as the status of women, the structure of the education system, the role of religion in government, the limits of social freedoms, and the definition of citizenship are not merely matters of public policy; they are essential elements of an order that the government is obliged to implement and protect.
For this reason, the expectation that the responsibilities of governing or international pressure would move the Taliban away from their ideological priorities was based on a misunderstanding of the movement’s nature. The international community assumed that governing would change the Taliban. The Taliban, however, viewed government as a means of transforming society according to their ideology. Perhaps the international community’s most fundamental analytical mistake was trying to understand the Taliban through the logic of states, while the Taliban viewed the state as an instrument for realizing their own ideological order.
New Political Status, Same Ideological Identity
The Doha negotiations and the Taliban’s return to power transformed the group’s political status, but they did not change its ideological identity. The Taliban evolved from an insurgent movement into an actor negotiating with major world powers, participating in diplomatic meetings, and becoming an unavoidable reality in regional politics. Yet a change in political status does not necessarily mean a change in a movement’s ideological foundations.
The Taliban’s ideological identity long pre-dated the Doha agreement, much less their return to power. It was shaped through decades of religious education, war, leadership structures, religious networks, and the narrative through which the Taliban defined their religious legitimacy and historical mission. For the Taliban, ideology was never a means of gaining power; rather, power was a means of advancing and expanding their ideology. For this reason, entering political negotiations or engaging with the international community did not necessarily mean reconsidering the movement’s fundamental objectives.
This misunderstanding, however, was not solely the product of the international community’s analytical framework. The Taliban themselves also played a role in shaping it. During the Doha negotiations, they sought to present a different image of themselves. The tone of Taliban representatives had changed, and they portrayed themselves as responsible actors, ready to engage with the international community and capable of governing Afghanistan. At the same time, by highlighting corruption, political divisions, and the failures of the former republic, they sought to present themselves as a legitimate alternative to the existing political order. 
Their official statements repeatedly referred to general amnesty, security, engagement with the international community, respect for the rights of women and minorities “within the framework of Sharia,” and balanced relations with other countries. Although these concepts were never clearly defined, their ambiguity reinforced the perception that the Taliban had changed since the 1990s.
Yet one fundamental question remains: Did the international community genuinely misunderstand the Taliban, or did ending the war and withdrawing from Afghanistan become such overriding political priorities that the existing understanding of the Taliban no longer served as the basis for policy? There is no simple answer to this question. The experience of Afghanistan, however, suggests that a significant gap existed between what was understood about the Taliban and the policies that were ultimately adopted toward them.
The Taliban’s rhetoric did not match their actions. While peace negotiations were underway, the group continued its military operations, recruitment, and expansion of its influence. As Afghanistan’s deputy minister of defense at the time, I witnessed firsthand that peace talks and intensified Taliban military operations were advancing simultaneously. This experience suggests that, when assessing an ideological movement, behavior on the ground is a more reliable indicator than the language of negotiations.
The Taliban’s conduct after returning to power revealed the same gap. The continuation of sweeping restrictions, the exclusion of much of the country’s independent professionals from government institutions, the strengthening of religious institutions, and the expansion of the authority of the Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice demonstrated that the Doha negotiations changed the international community’s calculations far more than they changed the Taliban.
What Should the World Learn for the Future?
Afghanistan’s experience challenges one of the most common assumptions underlying international peace processes: the belief that once an armed movement enters negotiations and later becomes part of the political order, it will gradually evolve into an actor compatible with the principles of modern governance. Afghanistan was not the first country in which this assumption was tested, and it is unlikely to be the last. 
If the most important conclusion of the past five years is simply that the Taliban have not changed, then the international community has learned very little from Afghanistan’s experience. But if this experience leads to a reconsideration of how peace processes are designed and how ideological movements are understood and engaged, then Afghanistan may become more than a national crisis; it may become one of the most important lessons for contemporary foreign policy.
First, no peace process should be built on the assumption that moving an ideological movement from the battlefield into political power will automatically transform it into an actor committed to democratic and accountable governance. Change should not be assumed at the negotiating table. It should be reflected in a movement’s behavior, institutional structure, sources of legitimacy, and practical acceptance of shared principles of governance.
articles.summary: The international community assumed that governing would change the Taliban. The Taliban, however, viewed government as a means of transforming society according to their ideology.

articles.title: Mecca Joint Deterrence Agreement: Implications for India
articles.full_text:
Pakistan would surely try to rally the group and invoke the pact in some form in the event of tensions with India.
Turkish President Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif hold copies of the Mecca Agreement after its signing on August 7, 2026.
On August 7, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye concluded the Mecca Joint Deterrence Agreement to strengthen “collective deterrence” against any act of aggression. The agreement states that an armed attack against “any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all.”
Signed in the holy city of Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, the pact expands the bilateral Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement (SMDA) between Riyadh and Islamabad signed in September 2025, to include Turkiye.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said more countries could join, potentially Egypt, though Cairo hasn’t responded. As per reports, Saudi Arabia has opposed Egypt’s inclusion due to President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s growing proximity with the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
Drawing a parallel to NATO’s Article 5 that calls for mutual defense, Fidan said the three signatories to the Mecca Agreement would decide through consultations the degree, form, and format of ​support they would request in the event of an attack.
The pact has raised several questions on its implications for India. While caution is advised, it shouldn’t be exaggerated for a variety of reasons.
The joint statement issued after the signing of the pact said that it was based on the enduring bonds of “brotherhood and Islamic solidarity” that unite the three countries and builds upon their “shared” strategic interests and longstanding defense cooperation, reflects their “shared commitment” to further strengthening “collective security” and to promoting peace, security, and stability in the “region and beyond,” in pursuit of a secure and prosperous future.
Fundamentally, the pact reflects the changing dynamics in the region and the decreasing confidence of West Asian countries in the U.S. It is their effort to build an alternative, rooted in the realization that emerged from the ongoing conflict in West Asia. Countries that have traditionally relied on the U.S. for their security have found themselves under attack from Iran, and the U.S. has proven unable to defend them. Further, hosting American bases that was earlier a guarantee of security has now become a liability. It made these countries vulnerable to attack. That Kuwait too has been negotiating an expanded defense agreement with Pakistan for deployment of troops and equipment in lieu of investments reinforces this perception.
It is unclear if the umbrella of Pakistan’s nuclear weapons, dubbed the “Islamic bomb,” would come under the Mecca pact. Last year, Pakistan’s Defense Minister Khawaja Mohammad Asif said the country’s nuclear program “will be made available” to Saudi Arabia if needed under the SMDA.
Pakistan is not new to such pacts and has a long history of providing military assistance to partners in the region. The 1982 Joint Defense Protocol saw the establishment of the Saudi-Pakistani Armed Forces Organization (SPAFO) and Pakistan stationed over 20,000 troops in Saudi Arabia. Similar cooperation has continued. Former Pakistan Army chief General Raheel Sharif commands the Saudi-led 2015 Islamic Military Alliance to Fight Terrorism in Yemen.
When Saudi Arabia faced attacks from Iran a few months back, Pakistan deployed 8,000 troops, a ​squadron of mostly JF-17 fighter jets and HQ-19 air defense system to Saudi Arabia under the SMDA. As per reports, the SMDA has provision for deployment of up to 80,000 troops.
In the past, Saudi Arabia has relied on Pakistan to fulfill its security requirements, and the latest pact is a continuation of that. In return, Pakistan remains on the right side of the influential Kingdom and gets much-needed financial aid, especially at a time when its economy is sinking.
Turkiye has long followed an independent policy and multilateral approach despite being a NATO partner. From a security perspective, Turkiye, despite significant military engagement with the U.S., has significantly scaled up its domestic defense industry, especially drones, and has been a supplier to both Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. Ankara brings this defense base and surge capacities, which have proven to be critical in recent conflicts, to the new pact.
Responding to the announcement of the Mecca pact, India said it continues to closely follow developments in West Asia conflict and, in particular, the “implications” of this pact, both from the perspective of national security as well as its implications for regional peace and stability. India remains fully committed to safeguarding its national interests and will take all necessary measures in this regard, Spokesperson of the Ministry of External Affairs Randhir Jaiswal said at a scheduled press briefing.
While the pact is more about regional dynamics, Pakistan will try to project and use it as a buffer in future tensions with India, especially after the bitter lessons during Operation Sindoor in May last year.
The 2016 surgical strikes by the Indian Army on militant camps across the Line of Control, a response to the terror attack in Uri, challenged the long-held perception that India would refrain from conventional operations for fear of Pakistan’s nuclear options. Similarly, in Operation Sindoor, a response to the attack on tourists in Pahalgam, India struck the heart of the military establishment following Pakistani strikes and established decisive military asymmetry. Indian long-range precision strikes on military targets between May 8-10, 2026, met with little resistance even as the HQ9 air defense systems were taken out and runways disabled. During the four-day conflict, Pakistan was actively aided by China and Turkiye. Pakistan extensively used Turkish drones to target Indian positions and test defenses and Turkish military operatives were believed to be on the ground assisting Pakistan.
Operation Sindoor sets a new precedent in escalation dynamics for the Indian sub-continent and arguably forced military planners in Rawalpindi to look for new strategies, both military and political.
While Operation Sindoor established India’s military edge, the narrative didn’t reflect that, especially with U.S. President Trump’s repeated claims of having mediated the ceasefire.
Since May 2025, the global geopolitical situation has significantly changed, with U.S. strikes on Iran, now a full-fledged conflict; uncertainties around the Strait of Hormuz and the changing contours of the war in Ukraine. Islamabad has positioned itself well through these developments. Coming on top of it, the defense pact does create uncertainties and merits caution on India’s part.
That said, it shouldn’t lead to unnecessary apprehensions.
There are several grey areas in the circumstances, criteria and procedures under which the collective defense provision in the Mecca pact may be invoked. That is likely a consultative and evolving process. For instance, in the event of India resorting to military action against Pakistan in response to a major terrorist attack, it is highly unlikely that Turkiye and Saudi Arabia would join militarily. Several Indian officials shared this view, while some observers also argued that India can play a more proactive security role in West Asia given its long-standing ties.
Similarly, are the ongoing tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan a fit criterion for invoking the collective defense provision? It is noteworthy that the Houthi drone strike on the Jazan refinery on August 9, just days after the pact was signed and caused no casualties, didn’t draw any joint response.
India-Saudi ties have also significantly deepened in recent years and as the Kingdom looks at diversification of its economy and security, India is an important pillar it wouldn’t want to lose.
Given the complexity of the relationships in the region and beyond and the evolving dynamics, for now the pact remains an expression of political intent and a hedging strategy rather than a decisive military bloc.

articles.title: Afghanistan: 5 Years in the Dark
articles.full_text:
How the Taliban turned Afghanistan into a country where half the population has been ordered to disappear.
Fatima keeps her medical textbooks in a cupboard she no longer opens. Her university ID card, with its photograph of a 19-year-old who intended to become a doctor, sits among them like a relic from another country. In a sense, it is. The Afghanistan that printed the card – a state with a constitution, a free press and women in its universities, courtrooms, and newsrooms – no longer exists.

In December 2022, women were expelled from every public and private university in the country. Women and Amnesty International warn that it effectively normalizes the marrying-off of children.

Consider the Hazaras, the country’s Shiite minority, comprising perhaps a fifth of the population. articles.title: Restrictions on Foreign Fund Flow to Christian Organizations in India Complicate India-US Ties
articles.full_text:
If the row over India’s proposed amendment of the FCRA persists alongside other irritants, the trade deal will remain in limbo for the foreseeable future.
On March 25, the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment (FCRA) Bill, 2026, was introduced in the Lok Sabha, the lower house of the Indian Parliament. The bill seeks to amend the FCRA Act 2010, which regulates the receipt and use of foreign contributions by individuals and organizations in India.
Since 2010, the act has been amended three times, most recently in 2020. A key provision of the recent amendment bill relates to the creation of a “designated authority” under the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), which has been empowered to provisionally take over, manage, and dispose of the assets of an organization if its FCRA registration is canceled, surrendered, or undergoes “deemed cessation” due to non-renewal. This change has generated considerable criticism. On August 12, parliament adopted a motion referring the bill to a 31-member joint parliamentary committee, which will scrutinize the bill and submit its report in the first week of the parliament’s winter session.
Beyond strong domestic criticism, especially from opposition parties, the bill has triggered a strong reaction from several American politicians, including Congressman Riley Moore, who slammed the bill as an “attack on Christians.” Senator James Risch, who heads the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee, described the proposed amendments as “deeply concerning” and said the U.S. would not “hesitate to call out countries who violate… human rights of Christians and other religious groups around the world.” In an opinion piece for the Washington Examiner in May, Congressman Chris Smith described the legislation as “designed to set up the expropriation of Indian Christians.”
Categorically rejecting such claims, India’s Ministry of External Affairs described the FCRA Amendment Bill as an “internal matter.” In a bid to alleviate Washington’s concerns, India’s Ambassador to the U.S. Vinay Mohan Kwatra took to social media to “debunk” certain “myths” surrounding the proposed bill. He said the bill seeks to improve transparency and make way for better governance and clearer rules. Kwatra highlighted how foreign contributions received by registered organizations in India have increased from $1.2 billion in 2010-11 to $2.67 billion in 2024-25.
Against this backdrop, U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor held back-to-back meetings early this week with Indian Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri and National Security Adviser Ajit Doval. While the specifics of their discussions were not revealed, the timing of the meeting suggests that it was an attempt to prevent the issue from snowballing into a diplomatic crisis.
Notably, Gor also intensified his outreach to states ruled by opposition parties; he held meetings with the chief ministers of Karnataka, Kerala, and Telangana. Both Karnataka and Telangana are ruled by the Congress party, which has been extremely vocal in its opposition to the FCRA. The Kerala Legislative Assembly has even passed a resolution urging the Union government to repeal the amendments to the FCRA, claiming they are “a breach of Constitutional provisions and federal principles.”
Critics of the amendment bill highlight that tighter controls could make it harder for legitimate organizations to access overseas funding. Archbishop Joseph Dsouza, president of the All-India Christian Council, described the amendment bill as “legalized loot of the Indian Christian community and the global Christian community.”
International Christian Concern, which describes itself as a Washington D.C.-based religious organization serving persecuted Christians worldwide, alleged that under the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government, Christian-aligned organizations in India are facing heightened scrutiny. It stated that more than 70 percent of NGOs whose licenses expired as of January 2022 were “aligned with Christian programs.”
In 2016, Compassion International, a Christian charity organization, was placed on a watchlist by India’s Ministry of Home Affairs due to suspected involvement in religious conversions. In response, the U.S. Foreign Affairs Committee held a full committee hearing, “American Compassion in India: Government Obstacles,” during which several members reprimanded the Indian government for restricting the charity’s operations in India. Compassion International claimed that Indian government restrictions prevented it from getting funds through to India, ultimately forcing it to wind up its work in the country in 2017.
In May this year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio began his four-day visit to India in Kolkata, visiting the Missionaries of Charity founded by Mother Teresa. After his visit, Rubio took to X to describe the mission as a “living example of the Catholic faith in action.” His visit to Kolkata, the first by a U.S. secretary of state in almost 14 years, sent a strong signal conveying that protection of American civil society assets in India remains a priority for the Trump administration. Back in December 2021, the FCRA license of the Missionaries of Charity was temporarily canceled, resulting in an international backlash and domestic criticism, forcing the government to restore the organization’s FCRA status on January 7, 2022.
The Indian government’s defense has been that such laws are not unique to India. Several countries, including the United States, have laws in place that regulate the flow of foreign funds. Several government representatives have repeatedly insisted that the law is “religion neutral” and that legitimate organizations have nothing to fear from the proposed amendments.
New Delhi says valid concerns underlie its restrictions on foreign funding to NGOs. In 2020, for instance, the Central Bureau of Investigation registered a case against a non-profit, Caruna Bal Vikas, for allegedly violating FCRA rules by engaging in activities that involved “converting poor children into fulfilled Christian adults.”
Evidently, the FCRA issue has been a lingering point of friction between India and the United States. While Washington often points to weaponization of FCRA by the BJP government to curtail freedom of association, New Delhi maintains that it is a necessary national security measure to prevent the use of foreign funds for activities that threaten India’s sovereignty.
With the FCRA issue back in the spotlight, the question it raises is: will this impact India-U.S. ties? Historically, by itself, this issue has not derailed ties since both sides recognize that the bilateral relationship is too consequential and broad-based.
However, given the changed circumstances under the second Trump administration, strained bilateral ties over trade tensions, repeated tariff threats, renewed U.S. engagement with Islamabad, among other things, may mean that this issue will add to the web of complications. Its most immediate impact may be in further delaying ongoing negotiations over the bilateral trade deal, the framework for which was first announced in February 2026.
Based on a Reuters report from July this year, the long-awaited agreement was expected to be signed within three to four months. If the FCRA row persists, alongside other irritants, the trade deal will remain in limbo for the foreseeable future.
During his first term, President Donald Trump made fighting Christian persecution around the world a foreign policy priority. Washington’s recent move allocating nearly $2 billion to “faith-based and community organizations” that provide global health and humanitarian assistance around the world reflects how religious freedom remains a foreign policy priority for his second term as well. Given that policymakers in Washington continue to view India’s legislative actions over the FCRA as restrictions on religious freedom, New Delhi cannot afford to ignore the friction without risking real damage to bilateral ties.

articles.title: The Key Takeaways From the Vietnamese President’s Visit to Australia
articles.full_text:
To Lam’s four-day trip marked a new high-water mark in the relationship between Hanoi and Canberra.
Vietnam and Australia released three joint statements at the conclusion of Vietnamese President To Lam’s state visit to Australia from August 9-12. The number and significance of these documents show that the two sides did more than exchange pleasantries, offering a clear indication of the upward trajectory in Vietnam-Australia relations.
The headline achievement of Lam’s visit was the signing of three separate joint statements: one on deepening the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership (CSP), one on economic resilience cooperation, and one on the enhancement of science, technology, and innovation connectivity. This is unprecedented; no previous visit by either country’s leader has produced three parallel statements.
The first statement is essentially political. It reaffirms the strategic trust built between the two nations over five decades and “the strength of the Viet Nam-Australia Comprehensive Strategic Partnership” that the two sides established in March 2024. President Lam and Prime Minister Albanese saw this as a reflection of “the increasing convergence of strategic interests and agreed that cooperation should be ambitious and forward-looking.”\
The second and third statements, by contrast, are more functional and forward-looking. That two of the three statements are devoted to economic resilience and technological cooperation reflects the priorities of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) and the Vietnamese government, which are pushing toward their stated goal of becoming a developed, high-income nation by 2045. They also signal a new shared driver of the bilateral relationship at a moment when global supply chains and technological competition are being reshaped by geopolitical volatility.
Perhaps the most striking language in the outcomes refers to the imperative of economic resilience. The two sides described this as “foundational to national security and prosperity,” and as touching on core “national interests.” Both countries expressed “concern over policies and practices that disrupt global supply chains or unnecessarily restrict trade,” and pledged to work together on resilience, on strengthening regional economic architecture, and on critical minerals.
That economic resilience issue rates its own standalone statement, separate from the broader CSP statement, underscores how central economic security has become to how both Hanoi and Canberra think about their national interests today. In the first statement, economic security is even broadly linked with “the critical role that straits used for international navigation and sea lanes of communication,, without naming any involved parties but implicitly referring to the ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and the situation in the South China Sea.
However, the third statement, on science, technology and innovation connectivity, may end up having the most long-term significance. Vietnam and Australia reaffirmed that this area is a pillar of the CSP, but went further by pledging deeper connectivity between the two countries’ innovation ecosystems. To make this happen, Lam and Albanese “agreed to explore opportunities for expanding joint research, strengthening links between their innovation ecosystems, and pursuing new collaborative initiatives.”
For Vietnam, this opens the potential of harnessing Australia’s advanced technology infrastructure and potential technology transfers – no small thing in a world where advanced economies are guarding their technological edge more closely. For Australia, the agreement offers a stronger foothold in a Southeast Asian partner whose economic and strategic weight is rising.
There is a broader logic at work here. Economic prosperity and national security, in the current environment, cannot be separated from capacity in science and technological innovation. By elevating this into a dedicated joint statement, Vietnam is effectively using a well-connected Western partner as a channel to access critical and strategic technologies it could not as easily obtain elsewhere. In other words, Australia is emerging as a trusted intermediary through which Vietnam can plug into the technological ecosystem of the developed world – a smart, low-friction route toward Vietnam’s own development ambitions.
Defense cooperation was also reinforced during Lam’s visit through an updated Joint Vision Statement on Further Defense Cooperation, under which the two countries’ defense ministers agreed to increase exchanges in military training, information sharing, military medicine, peacekeeping, search and rescue, and counter-terrorism. Maritime cooperation received particular attention, befitting two nations with substantial coastlines and maritime interests. The leaders also welcomed closer collaboration on maritime security, including intelligence-sharing, while also underscoring freedom of navigation and overflight, peaceful resolution of disputes, and adherence to the 1982 U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea in response to recent developments in the South China Sea.
Notably, the joint statements show that Vietnam is speaking with greater confidence about the “Indo-Pacific” as a regional construct; Hanoi has historically been more cautious in using the term than some of its partners. In a more assertive gesture, Hanoi and Canberra emphasized the importance of “strengthening collective capacity to respond to changing dynamics and emerging challenges in the Indo-Pacific region.” By aligning its language with Australia’s, and by extension with other proponents of the Indo-Pacific framing such as Japan and India, Vietnam is signaling its more assured positioning within this broader regional architecture, rather than treating the concept as belonging primarily to others.
Taken together, the three joint statements mark a new high-water mark in the Vietnam-Australia relationship. What stands out is not simply the volume of agreements but the underlying rationale that both sides have offered for them. This is a partnership described as resting on strategic trust and a genuine convergence of interests and security concerns, rather than one stitched together by circumstance or short-term calculation.
This suggests both Hanoi and Canberra now regard their closeness as something structural and enduring — a natural fit between a rising Southeast Asian economy seeking capital, technology and market access, and a resource-rich, technologically advanced partner seeking a stronger anchor in a dynamic region.
Whether this relationship is tempered by the pressures of a volatile world will depend on how well these intentions are put into practice. But as a statement of intent, the Canberra outcomes leave little doubt about where both governments want this relationship to go.

The two sides described this as “foundational to national security and prosperity,” and as touching on core “national interests.” Both countries expressed “concern over policies and practices that disrupt global supply chains or unnecessarily restrict trade,” and pledged to work together on resilience, on strengthening regional economic architecture, and on critical minerals.
That economic resilience issue rates its own standalone statement, separate from the broader CSP statement, underscores how central economic security has become to how both Hanoi and Canberra think about their national interests today. In the first statement, economic security is even broadly linked with “the critical role that straits used for international navigation and sea lanes of communication,, without naming any involved parties but implicitly referring to the ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and the situation in the South China Sea.
However, the third statement, on science, technology and innovation connectivity, may end up having the most long-term significance. Vietnam and Australia reaffirmed that this area is a pillar of the CSP, but went further by pledging deeper connectivity between the two countries’ innovation ecosystems. To make this happen, Lam and Albanese “agreed to explore opportunities for expanding joint research, strengthening links between their innovation ecosystems, and pursuing new collaborative initiatives.”
For Vietnam, this opens the potential of harnessing Australia’s advanced technology infrastructure and potential technology transfers – no small thing in a world where advanced economies are guarding their technological edge more closely. For Australia, the agreement offers a stronger foothold in a Southeast Asian partner whose economic and strategic weight is rising.
There is a broader logic at work here. Economic prosperity and national security, in the current environment, cannot be separated from capacity in science and technological innovation. By elevating this into a dedicated joint statement, Vietnam is effectively using a well-connected Western partner as a channel to access critical and strategic technologies it could not as easily obtain elsewhere. In other words, Australia is emerging as a trusted intermediary through which Vietnam can plug into the technological ecosystem of the developed world – a smart, low-friction route toward Vietnam’s own development ambitions.
Defense cooperation was also reinforced during Lam’s visit through an updated Joint Vision Statement on Further Defense Cooperation, under which the two countries’ defense ministers agreed to increase exchanges in military training, information sharing, military medicine, peacekeeping, search and rescue, and counter-terrorism. Maritime cooperation received particular attention, befitting two nations with substantial coastlines and maritime interests. The leaders also welcomed closer collaboration on maritime security, including intelligence-sharing, while also underscoring freedom of navigation and overflight, peaceful resolution of disputes, and adherence to the 1982 U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea in response to recent developments in the South China Sea.
Notably, the joint statements show that Vietnam is speaking with greater confidence about the “Indo-Pacific” as a regional construct; Hanoi has historically been more cautious in using the term than some of its partners. In a more assertive gesture, Hanoi and Canberra emphasized the importance of “strengthening collective capacity to respond to changing dynamics and emerging challenges in the Indo-Pacific region.” By aligning its language with Australia’s, and by extension with other proponents of the Indo-Pacific framing such as Japan and India, Vietnam is signaling its more assured positioning within this broader regional architecture, rather than treating the concept as belonging primarily to others.
Taken together, the three joint statements mark a new high-water mark in the Vietnam-Australia relationship. What stands out is not simply the volume of agreements but the underlying rationale that both sides have offered for them. This is a partnership described as resting on strategic trust and a genuine convergence of interests and security concerns, rather than one stitched together by circumstance or short-term calculation.
This suggests both Hanoi and Canberra now regard their closeness as something structural and enduring — a natural fit between a rising Southeast Asian economy seeking capital, technology and market access, and a resource-rich, technologically advanced partner seeking a stronger anchor in a dynamic region.
Whether this relationship is tempered by the pressures of a volatile world will depend on how well these intentions are put into practice. But as a statement of intent, the Canberra outcomes leave little doubt about where both governments want this relationship to go.
Vietnam and Australia released three joint statements at the conclusion of Vietnamese President To Lam’s state visit to Australia from August 9-12. The number and significance of these documents show that the two sides did more than exchange pleasantries, offering a clear indication of the upward trajectory in Vietnam-Australia relations.
articles.summary: To Lam's four-day trip marked a new high-water mark in the relationship between Hanoi and Canberra.

articles.title: Indonesia’s Transgender Community Is Facing Growing Repression
articles.full_text:
Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people as the government takes steps to codify anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law.
In October 2025, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto issued a presidential decree outlining the country’s national defense policy and the nonmilitary threats his administration identified as important to the nation’s security. Listed in the latter category, alongside terrorism, radicalism, and drug addiction, was “the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture,” as reported in the Jakarta Post.
While the decree drew concern from civil society organizations in Indonesia, particularly pro-democracy and queer rights groups, it initially received limited attention outside Indonesia. Last month, however, a wave of hate crimes targeted transgender women across the country, highlighting Prabowo’s decree and what activists have described as the worsening conditions for LGBTQ+ people in Indonesia.
Several transphobic incidents took place during July 14-16 of this year, all of which involved mobs attacking trans women specifically. In one particular instance in the West Java city of Bogor, over 15 trans women were doused with urine, forced to strip naked, and physically beaten in an incident that was recorded and later shared to social media. The online footage itself attracted more hate from some Indonesian netizens, who used slurs and called for further such attacks against trans people.
While Indonesia lacks explicitly anti-LGBTQ+ laws, several legal frameworks still indirectly discriminate against queer people, and stigma remains prevalent, largely as a result of conservative Muslim forces in the country. Transgender individuals are permitted to change their legal gender only if they have undergone sex reassignment surgery and subsequently received judicial approval. Same-sex sexual activities, meanwhile, can be criminalized under moral laws. The westernmost province of Aceh, the one Indonesian region governed by syariah law, stands as the most conservative on the issue, punishing homosexual acts with flogging, fines, or even jail time.
As such, Prabowo’s October 2025 decree represents a first step toward codifying anti-LGBTQ+ discrimination into federal law, using the language of securitization to justify this decision as necessary to preserve the peace, unity, and safety of Indonesia. According to Febi Ramadhan, a lecturer and researcher in social anthropology at Universitas Indonesia, this move is less than surprising. His research focuses on anti-LGBTQ+ discrimination in Indonesia’s political leadership, and highlights that such attitudes have significantly hardened over the last ten years.
“Starting in 2016, we saw a moral panic around queer people created by the government, sparked by proposed bills to criminalize LGBTQ+ behaviour, and key political leaders openly classifying queer identities as a form of mental illness,” he said. According to Febi, the transphobic attacks witnessed last month are just the latest such hate crimes to target the community, which have become more frequent over the past decade.
For Febi, periods of economic turmoil are key drivers of homophobia and transphobia in Indonesia, with queer people being demonized to divert attention from other issues the government doesn’t want to address or take responsibility for. In this case, the legacy of the nationwide 2025 protests, which saw large-scale public unrest as a result of the stagnating economy and sinking currency, is undoubtedly at play.
“At the same time, we have seen a shrinking of civil spaces across Indonesia, as a result of various laws restricting freedom of speech and assembly,” Febi added. “The community is facing the same crises again and again, but with diminishing resources, meaning we’re fighting several issues on many fronts at the same time.”
Among the laws targeting freedom of speech in the country, few have a bigger impact on public discourse than the Broadcasting Bill. In line with the government’s moral panic in 2016, the Indonesian Broadcasting Commission issued circulars explicitly banning television and radio stations from broadcasting content that features LGBTQ+ content, under the guise of protecting public morality and shielding children.
Rifki Lafayette, a queer Indonesian journalist, highlights how these restrictions have paved the way for the government’s further ​​amplification of anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes among the general public. “Professionally, there is a constant chilling effect: pitching a story addressing LGBTQ+ persecution will likely be killed by editors afraid of government reprisal or backlash from religious hardliners,” he said.
Rifki said that in order to avoid toeing the line and potentially face backlash from the government or their editors, many journalists choose to self-censor, cementing a culture of silence and taboo with regard to queer debates and issues.
He added that, over the years, the normalization of anti-LGBTQ rhetoric by the state has emboldened public vigilantes, who target and sometimes attack queer individuals, as was witnessed in Bogor. This, in turn, makes it more challenging for journalists like Rifki to report on LGBTQ+ stories in the field. “[We] are actively watched and scrutinized in public spaces, and if [we] are perceived to fit a queer stereotype, [we] risk immediate verbal harassment, being targeted with slurs, or the threat of physical intimidation from crowds,” he said.

Cornelius, who joined the nonprofit in 2023, described one of their key purposes as “making civil society more connected to the younger Gen​​ Z activists.” One such example was mobilizing resources for student activists during the anti-government protests in 2025.
With public sentiment now increasingly turning against trans people, Cornelius pointed to the dangers of public mobs and vigilantes, which has impacted the ways in which nonprofits like SJI can mobilize for the community. “During the 2016 moral panic, attacks came primarily from religious authorities and political leaders, but today those attacks are perpetrated by random individuals, which makes it hard for us to know who we are up against,” he said.

articles.title: Thailand Denies Reports It Planned to Use Security Cooperation as US Tariff Leverage
articles.full_text:
Bangkok has reaffirmed its commitment to the security relationship and denied a report that it was prepared to link military cooperation to ongoing trade talks.
The Thai government has denied reports that it plans to use military and security cooperation as leverage in its ongoing trade negotiations with the United States, reaffirming its commitment to the nations’ longstanding security relationship.
Rachada Dhanadirek, a spokesperson for the government, said on Wednesday that the talks would focus solely on how to attain fair and balanced trade between the two allies, Thai PBS reported.
Her comments came a day after a Bloomberg report stating that Thailand was preparing to warn the Trump administration that steep U.S. tariffs could force it to scale back military cooperation. This included the annual Cobra Gold joint exercises, a cornerstone of the U.S.-Thai alliance that have taken place since 1982.
The report quoted an unnamed Thai official familiar with the matter, who said this position was expected to form part of Thailand’s negotiating position in the reciprocal trade negotiations that are set to resume later this month.
“While the provision will be broadly worded,” the article stated, “Thailand could reconsider its participation in joint military activities if higher tariffs inflict significant economic damage.”
Rachada said yesterday that security cooperation would be quarantined from ongoing U.S. tariff negotiations and would not be used as leverage in the talks. She also said that existing military exchanges will proceed as planned, including Cobra Gold, the last iteration of which in February and March involved about 8,000 personnel from 30 countries.
“Thailand and the United States share broad and deep ties across many areas, including the economy, trade, security and people-to-people relations,” Rachada told the press. “Each area has its own framework and national interests that must be carefully considered. The government will not trade one national interest for another.”
Thailand has been negotiating a “reciprocal” trade deal with the U.S. since President Donald Trump’s initial “liberation day” tariff announcement in April 2025, when it was hit with a 36 percent tariff.
In October, the U.S. and Thailand announced a “framework” for an agreement on reciprocal trade, which reduced the tariff to a 19 percent tariff in exchange for a Thai pledge to “eliminate tariff barriers on approximately 99 percent of goods, covering a full range of U.S. industrial and food and agricultural products.” Under the framework, Thailand also promised to purchase more American energy, agricultural products, and aircraft in order to close its $71.9 billion goods trade surplus with the U.S.
However, the negotiation of a final agreement has been complicated and delayed by the seemingly constant shifts in U.S. tariff policy. In February, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the “liberation day” tariff regime, prompting Trump to impose a temporary 10 percent global tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act, which expired in July.
The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) has since used Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act of 1974, a provision that addresses unfair trading practices, as a way to reimpose the tariffs.
Thailand is among the 44 economies that the USTR threatened in June with a 12.5 percent tariff after concluding that they had taken insufficient steps to stop forced labor under Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act of 1974. It is also among 16 countries that the USTR has investigated for excess industrial capacity. The USTR has accused Thailand of “structural overcapacity” in three sectors: automotive and parts, machinery, and rubber products. If

Thailand has challenged both of these determinations, while offering to eliminate tariffs and adopt U.S. standards for imports of beef, lamb, and alcoholic beverages. Its negotiators have also pledged to introduce new legislation banning imports of goods made with forced labor.
As the Bloomberg report noted, Thailand is betting that its status as a U.S. treaty ally will guarantee it a slightly better deal than other Southeast Asian nations, such as Cambodia, Malaysia, and Indonesia, that have already established trade deals with the Trump administration. Commerce Minister Suphajee Suthumpun told The Nation last month that Thailand believed that it “has grounds to be treated on more favorable terms given the depth of the bilateral relationship,” in the newspaper’s paraphrase.
However, explicitly linking tariff talks to the security relationship, if indeed Thailand planned to do so, would have been a risky and provocative move given the volatile temper of the Trump White House and the uncertain state of the U.S.-Thai relationship. Since the end of the Cold War, the alliance has entered a state of drift, at the same time that Thailand has established increasingly close political, economic, and security ties to China – ties that have come under closer attention in Washington over the past decade.

articles.title: Former Myanmar Ambassador to UK Goes on Trial For ‘Trespassing’ in Diplomatic Residence
articles.full_text:
Kyaw Zwar Minn argues that the military government formed after the 2021 coup was illegitimate and had no authority to order him to vacate Myanmar House.
The Myanmar embassy to the United Kingdom in London, July 31, 2021.
Myanmar’s former ambassador to the United Kingdom appeared in a London court on Wednesday on trespassing charges for refusing to leave a diplomatic residence after being locked out of the embassy.
When the military seized power in a coup in February 2021, Ambassador Kyaw Zwar Minn denounced the takeover and pledged his loyalty to the opposition movement.
He was immediately dismissed by the junta and locked out of the embassy, but refused to leave Myanmar House, the ambassador’s official residence in northwest London. Kyaw Zwar Minn, now 68, has argued that Myanmar’s military government, which handed power to a “civilian” government in April of this year, was illegitimate and had no authority to ask him to vacate the property.
In May of last year, he was charged by London police last week with trespassing on a diplomatic premises between May 2021 and November 2024.
During the hearing at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday, Prosecutor Louise Oakley argued that he had been recalled as ​ambassador shortly after the 2021 coup, Reuters reported. She added that the military administration had ⁠instructed Kyaw Zwar Minn to “hand over state-owned properties” by the middle of April 2021, and that Britain’s Foreign Office has also told him to leave the residence.
“Having been granted permission to reside at Myanmar House as the ambassador, his refusal to vacate the diplomatic premises after he was removed ​from that position means that ​he is guilty ⁠of the offense of diplomatic trespass,” Oakley said.
Kyaw Zwar Minn’s lawyer David Perry told the court that his client’s case was that “the government ​of Myanmar is illegitimate” and that it “could not lawfully terminate his license at ​the (diplomatic) address,” nor “legitimately use the property.”
Oakley argued that the National Unity Government, the opposition umbrella group to which Kyaw Zwar Minn has aligned himself, has not been recognized by London, even if many democratic nations have sanctioned the post-coup government and downgraded their representation in the country.
“This defendant may not recognize the outcome of the coup and the construction of ​the government in Myanmar – that, we submit, is irrelevant,” she said.
Among those who gave evidence on Wednesday was Win Zeyar Tun, chargé d’affaires at the Myanmar Embassy in London, and Eleanor Mackewn, the deputy director of protocol at the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office.
After the coup, some British officials praised Kyaw Zwar Minn’s principled opposition to the coup, which the U.K. government also forcefully condemned. However, his continued occupation of Myanmar House has presented it with a diplomatic headache.
As the BBC’s diplomatic correspondent James Landale pinpointed in an April 2021 report, the Vienna Convention on diplomatic relations states that an ambassador’s job officially ends once the host country has been informed of the change. However, by accepting that Kyaw Zwar Minn has been dismissed by his host government, the U.K. might “face accusations that it is tacitly accepting the authority of the regime in Myanmar,” Landale wrote.
Initially, the U.K. government sought to take a middle road. When the military junta requested that the authorities evict Kyaw Zwar Minn by force, the government declined to do so, instead urging the envoy to find alternative accommodation. His refusal to do more or less forced the authorities to press charges.
While Kyaw Zwar Minn benefited from a surge of sympathy in the wake of the coup, attention on the country has faded to a large extent over the past five years. This means that the U.K. government is unlikely to face much reputational damage if it forced to evict him and turn the property over to officials loyal to Naypyidaw. The moral force of Kyaw Zwar Minn’s argument, and the legal requirements of the Vienna Convention, suggest that his days in Myanmar House may be numbered.
The trial is to resume at Westminster Magistrates Court on September 25.

articles.title: How Indonesia Can Get Ahead in the Artificial Intelligence Race
articles.full_text:
The country has the abundant land and energy resources needed to power hyperscale data centers. Can it harness them effectively?
Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming economies around the world, but much of the discussion about it focuses on software, algorithms, computing power, regulation, and talent. While these factors are important, they overlook the one major precondition upon which everything else depends: a reliable supply of electricity.
Every AI application ultimately runs inside an AI data center and requires industrial land, electrical substations, cooling systems, fiber-optic connectivity, backup power, and, depending on the cooling technology employed, significant quantities of water. Without this infrastructure and the energy to power it, even the most advanced AI software, algorithms, and talent cannot be deployed at scale.
For Indonesia, this raises an important strategic question: Does it have the land, infrastructure, and energy needed to become a leading destination for AI investment? The answer will help determine whether Indonesia becomes a regional AI hub or watches investment flow elsewhere.
The Energy Bottleneck in Digital Infrastructure
AI is rapidly becoming as dependent on energy as it is on technology. Training advanced AI models requires vast numbers of specialized processors operating continuously for weeks or months. Even after models have been trained, serving millions of AI queries each day creates a permanent and growing demand for electricity. The newest AI data centers already consume hundreds of megawatts of power, while some planned facilities are expected to consume as much electricity as medium-sized cities.
In this regard, Indonesia possesses several important advantages. It has Southeast Asia’s largest economy, a population approaching 300 million people, a rapidly expanding digital economy, growing cloud adoption, and government policies that recognize AI as a national priority. Unlike Singapore, where land and energy have become increasingly scarce, Indonesia has abundant industrial land, substantial natural gas resources, and one of the world’s largest geothermal resource bases.
The country currently has approximately 580 megawatts of operational AI data center capacity, with more than 1.3 gigawatts of additional capacity announced or under development. Much of this expansion is being driven by growing demand for AI, cloud computing, and digital services, with investment concentrated around Greater Jakarta, West Java, and Batam.
The largest hyperscale data center developers in Indonesia are now negotiating electricity supply years before construction begins. They are seeking dedicated substations, transmission infrastructure, reserved generating capacity, and long-term power purchase agreements. BDx, one of Indonesia’s largest data center developers, recently secured commitments totaling approximately 1.2 gigawatts of electricity for future AI campuses in West Java. This illustrates the scale of electricity that future AI infrastructure will require.
Energy analysts have warned that reserve margins on the Java-Madura-Bali grid could fall below recommended levels by 2027 if sufficient new generating capacity is not brought online. As more data centers are developed, they will require significant amounts of electricity that households and industry could otherwise need. This could create political resistance if data centers are seen as contributing to higher electricity costs or reduced reliability, while making alternative power solutions more attractive.
Here Indonesia possesses another strategic advantage: large natural gas developments and one of the world’s largest undeveloped geothermal resource bases. Instead of viewing these resources solely as sources of electricity for the national grid or LNG exports, they could become the foundation for a new generation of AI infrastructure. While Indonesia is unlikely to manufacture the advanced AI processors used in these facilities, it has the potential to provide the physical infrastructure and energy needed to support them.
Several major gas developments are either under construction or entering expansion phases. These include the Masela LNG project operated by INPEX, the Tangkulo gas development operated by Mubadala Energy, BP’s expansion of the Tangguh LNG project, and ENI’s North and South Hub developments in the Kutei Basin. Together, these projects will substantially increase Indonesia’s future natural gas production and its ability to generate electricity.
Traditionally, natural gas produced in remote locations has been processed primarily into LNG for export. Some gas has also been used to support fertilizer and petrochemical industries, as well as on-site power generation. Instead of allocating a portion of that gas to fertilizer and petrochemical production, it could be used to generate electricity for hyperscale AI data centers located adjacent to LNG facilities.
Natural gas also provides reliable dispatchable power that can operate around the clock while offering lower greenhouse gas emissions, making it well suited to support energy-intensive AI infrastructure. Additionally, using a portion of Indonesia’s natural gas resources to power high-value AI infrastructure could create a new domestic industry while minimizing the need for major new infrastructure.
Locating AI data centers close to LNG developments provides several key advantages. Much of the required industrial land, utilities, ports, and supporting infrastructure already exist or are planned. The data center and its dedicated independent power producer could be developed as part of the same complex or jointly with the LNG operator, providing reliable captive electricity without requiring a new grid connection or placing additional demand on an existing grid. This integrated model also minimizes community disruption, streamlines permitting, and provides developers with a site that reduces both development costs and construction timelines compared with building entirely new AI campuses.
In addition to LNG capacity, Indonesia possesses some of the world’s largest geothermal reserves. Many remain undeveloped because they are located far from major centers of electricity demand, and developing them often requires substantial upfront transmission investment, making otherwise attractive projects uneconomic.
Instead of transmitting electricity over long distances, AI data centers could be built adjacent to geothermal power plants, consuming power at the source as dedicated off-takers. Geothermal energy provides continuous baseload electricity with capacity factors commonly exceeding 85 percent while offering domestic energy security, minimal greenhouse gas emissions, and the long-term price stability sought by hyperscalers pursuing low-carbon operations. Unlike natural gas, which must balance competing demands from LNG exports, domestic industry, fertilizer production, and power generation, geothermal has relatively few competing commercial uses beyond electricity generation, making it particularly well suited to supporting large-scale AI infrastructure.
The principal limitation of locating AI infrastructure at remote gas fields or geothermal developments is latency. Many AI applications require near-instantaneous responses and therefore need to be located close to major population centers. AI model training has very different operating requirements. Training large language models requires months of continuous computation across thousands of GPUs and is largely insensitive to modest network delays. Likewise, high-performance computing, scientific simulations, genomic research, and other compute-intensive workloads can operate effectively from remote locations where electricity is abundant and inexpensive.
Urban data centers serving AI inference and cloud services could continue to cluster around Greater Jakarta and other major cities. At the same time, remote AI training facilities could be developed alongside LNG projects and geothermal fields, where they would support AI training, high-performance computing, scientific research, and other energy-intensive computing workloads. Together, these two models could form the foundation of Indonesia’s future AI infrastructure.
Navigating Regional Competition and Implementation
Indonesia is not alone in competing for AI investment. Malaysia is also positioning itself as a regional data center hub, while Singapore continues to attract premium digital infrastructure despite constraints on land and energy. Indonesia’s advantage lies in its combination of abundant industrial land, large domestic energy resources, a growing digital economy, and the potential to develop dedicated captive power systems at a scale few countries in Southeast Asia can match.
For Indonesia, this presents a strategic opportunity. The country could use a portion of its natural gas and geothermal resources to power high-value AI infrastructure while continuing to support traditional industries such as LNG, fertilizer, petrochemicals, and domestic electricity generation. Geothermal and natural gas developments could become the basis for a new generation of AI campuses powered by dedicated captive electricity systems developed alongside the energy projects themselves.
This opportunity will require coordinated investment well beyond electricity generation. Supporting infrastructure such as high-capacity transmission networks, including high-voltage direct current where economically justified, expanded domestic and international fiber-optic connectivity, reliable water resources (supported where necessary by recycling or desalination), and modern digital infrastructure will all be important.
Indonesia will also need to balance competing demands for natural gas, continue modernizing its electricity system, and maintain a stable regulatory environment that encourages long-term private investment.
The global competition for AI is increasingly a competition for land, infrastructure, and energy. Countries that can deliver on these fundamentals will attract the next generation of hyperscale AI investment. Indonesia possesses many of the advantages needed to compete, but its success will depend on whether it can convert those advantages into commercial developments.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming economies around the world, but much of the discussion about it focuses on software, algorithms, computing power, regulation, and talent. While these factors are important, they overlook the one major precondition upon which everything else depends: a reliable supply of electricity.
Every AI application ultimately runs inside an AI data center and requires industrial land, electrical substations, cooling systems, fiber-optic connectivity, backup power, and, depending on the cooling technology employed, significant quantities of water. Without this infrastructure and the energy to power it, even the most advanced AI software, algorithms, and talent cannot be deployed at scale.
For Indonesia, this raises an important strategic question: Does it have the land, infrastructure, and energy needed to become a leading destination for AI investment? The answer will help determine whether Indonesia becomes a regional AI hub or watches investment flow elsewhere.
The Energy Bottleneck in Digital Infrastructure
AI is rapidly becoming as dependent on energy as it is on technology. Training advanced AI models requires vast numbers of specialized processors operating continuously for weeks or months. Even after models have been trained, serving millions of AI queries each day creates a permanent and growing demand for electricity. The newest AI data centers already consume hundreds of megawatts of power, while some planned facilities are expected to consume as much electricity as medium-sized cities.
articles.summary: The country has the abundant land and energy resources needed to power hyperscale data centers. Can it harness them effectively?

articles.title: How Could the Rise of Progressive Democrats Impact US China Policy?
articles.full_text:
A divide over China, although less pronounced than the divide over Israel, has become increasingly visible among Democrats as progressives have risen within the party.
U.S. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez attends a session at the Munich Security Conference, Feb. 14, 2026.
From Analilia Mejia to Abdul El-Sayed to Peggy Flanagan, a progressive winning streak in Democratic primaries has swept across the country in the lead-up to this year’s midterm elections. Unlike most midterm election cycles, where domestic issues dominate the political agenda, foreign policy has been thrust into the spotlight this time, with the Israel-Palestine conflict emerging as the defining litmus test of the Democratic Party. As progressive candidates have rallied behind the Palestinian cause in their battles against AIPAC-backed moderates, the party’s leftward ideological shift could impact not only the decades-long Israel-U.S. alliance, but also Washington’s policy toward its greatest strategic competitor: China. 
Progressives perceive the world through the lens of structural inequality. That worldview lies at the heart of their dissatisfaction with the status quo of the U.S. socioeconomic structure: a widening gap between economic elites and ordinary people. As a result, they fight against corporate interests and political corruption, thereby translating their opposition to economic elites into opposition to the political establishment. The same logic applies to foreign affairs – progressives can readily translate their anti-establishment sentiment into opposition to American primacy, which has long been buttressed by bipartisan support for U.S. military dominance. 
This helps explain why Palestine has become such a powerful cause on the left. Progressives tend to view U.S.-backed Israel as an extension of American power in the Middle East and Palestinians as victims of U.S. hegemony. Hence, although a parallel anti-Israel sentiment can also be seen among some Republicans, progressive Democrats have a fundamentally different motivation for their opposition to Israel. Whereas growing Republican opposition to unlimited aid to Israel is rooted largely in “America First” nationalism and isolationism, progressives seek to challenge American exceptionalism and the so-called U.S. global leadership that they believe perpetuates inequality. 
Today, the rise of China is increasingly portrayed as a challenge to the U.S.-led global order. As a result, neither Republicans nor Democrats can easily depart from the bipartisan consensus that Beijing represents Washington’s greatest strategic competitor. Whoever is perceived as “soft on China” is almost certain to face attacks from the other side of the aisle. Both parties have thus become more inclined to play the “China card” whenever they deem it necessary – either to inoculate themselves against accusations of weakness or to gain a political advantage. 
But the divide over China, although less pronounced than the divide over Israel, has become increasingly visible among Democrats with the rise of progressives. One vision, exemplified by establishment figures such as former President Joe Biden, sees a world defined by strategic competition, in which China-U.S. confrontation is unavoidable across a range of domains, from the economy and technology to culture. The other, exemplified by progressives such as Senator Bernie Sanders, rejects the self-fulfilling logic of the Thucydides Trap and champions a China policy centered on restraint and cooperation.
This progressive vision was on display in the remarks on Taiwan made by Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, known widely as AOC, at the Munich Security Conference this year. Despite her stumbles, AOC – arguably the biggest star among the progressive camp – captured an ethos fundamentally different from a competition-based China policy. Rather than stressing how the United States would defend Taiwan and democracy through strength, as many centrist Democrats might, she emphasized the need to work toward ensuring that the United States and China “never get to that point.”
Although it may still take time for AOC to take the national stage as a leading voice on foreign policy, her remarks epitomize a core tenet of progressive policy toward China: diplomacy before militarism. 
Yes, progressives condemn China for its human rights abuses, lack of genuine democracy, and unfair trade practices. But they also hold that, instead of beating the drums for a new Cold War with the Asian powerhouse, the United States should press these issues through bilateral dialogue and multilateral institutions such as the World Trade Organization and the U.N. Human Rights Council. They understand that the effectiveness of such diplomacy depends on the moral legitimacy of the American state, both at home and on the global stage. Only in this way can the United States strengthen its ability to marshal diplomatic pressure on China when necessary, not only on its own behalf but also on behalf of its allies around the world. 
For all intents and purposes, progressives are trying to build that moral legitimacy by reshaping the ideology of the Democratic Party. Nowhere is this more evident than in their challenge to the conventional U.S. support for Israel. This July, more than half of House Democrats voted to support cutting $3.3 billion in U.S. aid to Israel – a shift that would have been difficult to imagine ten years ago.
House Democrats’ new stance on Israel has a more profound implication: it could allow Congress to reclaim some of its authority over foreign policymaking from an increasingly power-hungry Donald Trump and hold policymakers accountable for poor foreign-policy decisions.
This matters because of the notoriously self-forgiving nature of the U.S. foreign policy establishment. Policymakers who make consequential mistakes can often walk away scot-free, regardless of their partisan affiliation. China policy has become one of the areas most vulnerable to this dynamic. On the Republican side, we have seen Trump’s relentless use of tariffs as a weapon against China. From the 145 percent “Liberation Day” tariffs in 2025 to the most recent 12.5 percent tariffs on Chinese imports, his aggressive use of tariffs has drawn criticism not only from Democrats but increasingly from Republicans as well. Yet Trump has continued to impose tariffs with little meaningful constraint from Congress. 
On the Democratic side, then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan in 2022, despite opposition from the Biden administration, likewise drew little public criticism from Democrats. The closest thing to a critique came from progressive Democrats such as Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders, who chose simply to remain silent.
But progressives could change that. Instead of being constrained by so-called party unity, they could translate their ideological commitments into concrete policies to check abuses of executive power in foreign policy. 
Take trade policy, for example. Progressives can connect it to their broader critique of wealth inequality in the United States. Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, illustrated this approach by framing tariffs as part of a larger conflict between working-class Americans and concentrated corporate interests. If enacted, the bill would curb Trump’s unfettered tariff powers and put Congress back in the driver’s seat on U.S. trade policy, potentially reshaping China-U.S. economic relations in the process. 
As the 2028 presidential election nears, the “China card” is very likely to be played with increasing frequency.
